items.s: THE 5 MILES JUNIOR CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Report and result of the club five miles junior cross-country championship for the "Savage" Shield on December 21st, won by E. Stimpson from D. Martin and G. R. Chantler. On December 21st our "Junior" Championship was held to decide who should become the holder of the "Savage" Shield for the ensuing year; and the paucity of entrants was more than compensated for by the quality of the racing. George Chantler (the holder), Dave Martin, Ed Stimpson and Ken Wood were always close together; but in the closing stages Stimpson found a little extra speed to finish nine seconds ahead of Martin. Chantler followed three seconds later, with Wood another 12 seconds away. Thus the fourth man finished only 24 seconds behind the winner, and shows what a splendid chance we have of retaining the "Southern" Junior title in February. We have, of course, three members of last year's winning team still available, and backed up by Wood, Chamberlain, Quackenbos, Merryman and Pointer, they can scarcely fail to do well. It is a source of great satisfaction to us to know that we have such splendid talent maturing and fitting itself for the senior ranks in due course. m. s. 1 E. Stimpson 30 16 2 D. Martin 30 25 3 G. items.s: BOXING DAY TRACK MEETING. Report of the club's annual Boxing Day handicap meeting at Battersea Park track on a heavy track: 120 yards sprint won by T. H. Cannon, 2 miles won by A. A. Bird, 3 miles walk won by L. F. Bailey. Our annual Boxing Day meeting was held at Battersea Park Track, as usual, and the track was very heavy, owing to the continuous rains. The entries for the 120 yards sprint were much better than last year, and when the five heat winners lined up for the final, an expectant crowd awaited the result. T. H. Cannon (11) proved the winner off a mark he will certainly not see again, with F. W. Pritchard (8), second, and K. J. Crawford (10) third. Our young Junior Sprint Champion, B. Saunders, qualified for the final but was unplaced, as was Frank Webb. The 2 Miles Run proved a good race and after George Still had shown the way in the early stages, A. T. A. Jordan (300) took the lead only to lose it in a thrilling struggle down the straight to A. A. Bird (250). J. C. Edwards (350) finished third, with A. H. Beaumont (280) 4th, G. Still (650) 5th. A. R. Shaw ran well off 95 yds. to finish 6th. A. W. Penny, our Empire Games 6 Miles Champion, turned out but was content to finish 12th, his time being 10 mins. 5 secs. The time of the winner was 9 mins. 43 secs., and considering the heavy going this was quite a sound performance. In the 3 Miles Walk we saw a fine performance by Len Fletcher who, off 20 yds., finished second to L. F. Bailey (600). Charlie Speechley (275) gained third place with J. E. Rutland (300) 4th, Harry Churcher (65) 5th, and Colin Sutton (300) 6th. The winner's time was 22 mins. 6 secs., while Fletcher clocked 22 mins. 18 secs., a remarkable effort in view of the state of the track. T. H. Cannon T. H. Cannon won 120 yards sprint off 11 F. W. e: Surrey County Junior Cross Country Championships
items.s: THE COUNTY CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIPS. Report and results of the 1935-36 county cross-country championships: Belgrave's fourth successive Surrey team win with Arthur Penny individual champion, Cadogan A.C. third in Middlesex with E. S. Stimpson winning the junior race, Pat Parker Sussex champion, and the club third in the Surrey junior championship. The Surrey race, held at Epsom, provided us with our fourth successive win, and once again we supplied the individual champion. We has expected to do both of these things, but Arthur Penny had a gruelling race with S. C. Belton (Surrey A.C.) in order to regain the Surrey title. Belton was a real thorn in Arthur's side, and it was only in the closing stages that our man was able to open up a small gap and hold it to the end. Third came the old warrior, Bert Footer, running one of his "waiting" races, and showing that will be with the leaders when the "Southern" and "National" come along. Our third man was Tom Carter, in 8th position. He ran very creditably in view of his short preparation, following on a minor accident which had put him out of the game for nearly a month. Next for us came Syd Ring, striving to put every second possible between himself and the following men; then Bert Cook, the evergreen; and "Mick" Walker. We thus finished our six in the first 19 scoring positions. Surrey A.C.'s sixth man scored 21, so it will be seen that our win was by no means an easy one. Every man had to do his bit to enable us to score 53 points to the 77 of Surrey A.C. It will be remembered that it was in this race last year that Arthur Penny fractured his meta-tarsial bone, which resulted in him being an onlooker until this season started. It was pleasing to see him re-assume one of his old titles and show that he is as good as ever. In the Middlesex race held from Enfield Lock, our members competing encountered a real cross-country course, with more than its share of hills and mud. In the last two years Cadogan A.C. (whose members are all first-claim Belgrave Harriers) had won the team title; but this time had to strike their flag, not altogether unexpectedly. The team was well-beaten by Southgate H. and Polytechnic H., and next year our lads will be all out to regain their lost title. In the absence of D. and R. Patience abroad on Foreign service we knew things would be more difficult, but with Ginty unable to run owing to ankle trouble, and Saunders arriving late following a motor-cycle breakdown, Cadogan A.C. were certainly up against it! The course was certainly not to Arthur Allum's liking, and Alf Taylor took over Arthur's usual role of leading the team in. In all the circumstances third team placing must be considered creditable, and is sure to spur our men on to something better next year. The Senior race had been preceded by the Junior event over five miles, and in this E. S. Stimpson distinguished himself by showing splendid form throughout, and winning comfortably. He should help our seniors along next year. Our only other runner in this was H. M. Quackenbos, who was placed 16th of the 51 starters—quite a good effort. Pat Parker carried off the Sussex individual title which was competed for at Hassocks ,and Bert Shaw took fourth place in the Kent championship. A week after the Surrey County Senior Championship, the Junior event was held from St. George's Services S. Club's quarters at Raynes Park. It must be confessed that our Juniors rather disappointed by only finishing third to South London Harriers, and Mitcham A.C. However, no doubt they have something in reserve for the Southern Junior Championship. We can depend upon them to train on and do their utmost to retain this title for the Club. 53 individuals finished. 8 teams closed in. m. s. m. s. 1 A. Perny 40 58 25 C. Penny 43 45 2 S. C. items.label: February 1936
items.sum: Preview of the club's remaining 1936 winter fixtures: a social run with Herne Hill, the South of Thames championship, Southern and National (English) cross-country championships, the Round Ilford Relay, the club 5 miles road race and the Brighton Relay.
e: South of Thames Cross Country Championship
items.s: WINDING UP THE WINTER SEASON. Preview of the club's remaining 1936 winter fixtures: a social run with Herne Hill, the South of Thames championship, Southern and National (English) cross-country championships, the Round Ilford Relay, the club 5 miles road race and the Brighton Relay. On February 1st we are visiting the Herne Hill Harriers for a social run from the Grandstand, Epsom Downs. The surrounding country will by now be quite familiar to our boys; but it is a fine, healthy spot for running, and I recommend it to any of our members who have as yet not sampled it. On February 8th we have the South of Thames 7 Miles C.C. Championship which will be held at Dartford. The last time this race was held there, Bert Footer won the individual title, while our team was placed second in the team race. We hope to go one better this time by securing first place in the team event, although Reading A.C. appear to have an excellent chance of improving on their second place of last year. Unfortunately, most of our cracks are barred from competing, but we have some most promising talent in our junior ranks and know that our boys will not fail through lack of effort. We have a fixture with St. George's Services A.C. on February 15th. Our Surrey Juniors have already been over the course, which is from the L.C.C. Technical School Playing Fields, Grand Drive, Raynes Park. Our team will be of Junior strength and this should give those who are not concerned with our Senior teams a chance of competition late in the season. February 22nd is Southern Counties Day, and both the Senior and Junior races will be held at Sandown Park. The last time the race was held here was in 1886, when the field numbered 181 competitors. This year the field for the Junior race will exceed that number, while over 300 runners are likely to be seen in the Senior event, a sure proof of the growing popularity of cross-country running as a sport. The surrounding country should make for an interesting race and our lads should not be at a disadvantage over this type of course. It should be a most hectic fight between Surrey A.C., the holders, and the "Bels"; and with memories of our one-point defeat last year, our lads can be relied upon to go all out to avenge that reverse. Our Junior team is if anything stronger than last year, and we should certainly retain our title of Southern Junior Champions. Ted Stimpson is running brilliantly, and with Dave Martin, George Chantler, K. N. Wood and J. W. Chamberlain to give their support, they should improve on last year's score. Travelling arrangements will be published at a later date, and will also be placed on the notice board at the "Rising Sun." Spectators should have a fine view of both races and we hope our followers will make the journey. For the following two weeks we have training runs at Wimbledon, when our team will be having their final preparation for the National race on March 14th. THE ENGLISH C.C. CHAMPIONSHIP, of which we are holders, will be held over a 10 miles course in Alderley Park, Cheshire, on March 14th, at 3-15 p.m. I hope that many of our followers will make the journey. It is surprising how it helps to hear a word of encouragement every now and again, especially in a race over 10 miles. Birchfield Harriers will strain every sinew to regain their lost honours; while Surrey A.C. and Salford Harriers are also sure to be well to the fore. This race was held at Alderley Edge in 1933, and Bert Footer and Arthur Penny came in together in 4th position. If they can repeat that performance (and on present form it looks highly likely) we shall have made a good start for team honours. Jim Ginty has now commenced training, and although we shall miss Dan Patience, who is in Egypt; Tom Carter, Alf Taylor and Harry Shields are showing form that gives every promise of their repeating last year's magnificent performance. It is a pity that Pat Parker will not be eligible for our team, nor of course Les Cohen; but even so I am confident that our lads can show the athletic world that Belgrave are supreme over the country. On March 21st will be held the Round Ilford Relay race, of which we are the holders, and at the time of writing it is uncertain what the composition of our team will be. I am sure our "B" team enjoyed their run last year and it may be decided to let them have a crack at the others on their own. A fortnight later, April 4th, we are holding our usual end-of-the-season 5 Miles Road race at Wimbledon. We have a Sealed Handicap open to all members in conjunction with this race; and it serves for those who have kept in steady training all through the Winter season. The result of the scratch race is also used when selecting our team for the Brighton Relay race, which takes place three weeks later. All those who wish to be considered for this race should make a point of being at Wimbledon on April 4th. On referring to the fixture card you will notice that the date of our Road Race has been altered, but this is owing to the Brighton Relay date being brought forward. APRIL 25th, Brighton Relay Day. I had better not say London to Brighton, as according to what we hear the race is due to start anywhere between Mitcham and Dorking. One thing is certain, and that is that the Commissioner of Police has forbidden it to start from Westminster, as in years past. It seems rather a pity, as it robs the event of the interest taken in the carrying by the runners of a letter from the Lord Mayor of London to his counterpart at Brighton. I expect Joe Binks, with his usual slick publicity methods will soon get another to replace this, but at the time of writing all we know is that the race will be held, but that's about all. Anyway, sailors don't care, so why should we? One thing we do know, that this race provides a good day's outing for both young and old; and I am sure all our lads look forward to it as one of the season's most sporting events. Incidentally, if our boys can win again this year they will put up a record by winning the event three years in succession. Birchfield have twice had successive wins but so far no club has done the treble, so up the "Bels," and do your stuff! Entries and enquiries should be sent to— E. A. DUFFETT, Asst. Hon. Sec., 10, Barrow Road, Waddon, Surrey. items.label: February 1936
items.sum: Humorous account by A. S. Lindsey of the club's third Social of the season on December 14th, with the burlesque show "Belgrave Nights" or "East of Wapping" starring A. A. Harley as Sheik El Red.
items.s: "BELGRAVIAN NIGHTS." Humorous account by A. S. Lindsey of the club's third Social of the season on December 14th, with the burlesque show "Belgrave Nights" or "East of Wapping" starring A. A. Harley as Sheik El Red. The third Social of the season was held on December 14th. A fair number stayed to tea and were supplemented later by others eager to dance, and to see the show which we were promised. Unfortunately, the band engaged was late, and things had to be got going; and this is where our Hon. Secretary, Wally, stepped up. He did some good work on the ivories, assisted with great gusto by the company present. Eventually the band materialised, and after a short period of dancing we came to the attraction of the evening—"Belgrave Nights" or "East of Wapping." The curtain rose (if one may use the term) depicting the splendour of the East, with Sheik El Red (A. A. Harley) reclining on a divan, looking a veritable Bluebeard all gone bloodshot. (Note: in our last presentation, "Love in Bloom," it will be remembered that our esteemed Hon. Editor was then only a back-row girl. Well done, Red!). At the Sheik's side towered his Nubian (bleached) slave, Ali Ben Mai, a colossal heap of flesh, but none the less an honest fellow, who calls a blade a blade. At the Master's bidding, Ali ushered in the Court musicians (Jack and Charlie) who gave a good account of themselves on the accordions, and were awarded long and uproarious applause. Next came a slave girl (Percy Wright), a beautiful maiden from the East (End!), but with Ali it was a case of see blondes and bust! Sallying forth, he literally proceeded to knock the stuffing out of the maiden. After this bout (which Ali won by three throws to nil), the slave girl entertained us with a snake dance; a string of best beef sausages taking the place of the snake. To keep the Royal pot a-boiling, Ali, with a few passes of his (t)rusty blade, persuaded the Court singer (T. Cotton) to entertain. Of course, Tom always goes down well. Unfortunately, you can't keep a good man down for long! After this, the Court musicians got busy again, and to the strains of Eastern music, the Neverwere Dancers entered, presenting a very native dance dedicated to their patron, St. Vitus. This part of the show was under the personal supervision of Miss J. Parsons, whom we all thank for her patience and interest. An easier task would be training elephants to walk the tight-rope, and the chances of success would be greater! Alf. Taylor and A. A. Bird should go far; I am on safe ground in saying the like has never been seen before! "Mick" Walker and "Snaky" Webb, whose dancing reputations are far-flung, should play opposite one another, more often if possible. Ring, the Ruthless, gave a great exhibition of Eastern passion in contrast to his partner, Cecil Penny, who danced with utter abandon. La Josephine, and our friend Ali, put in some fine work, although I am inclined to think the scales were faked when they weighed in! The performance was seasonably concluded by El Red distributing presents on behalf of generous-hearted Belgravians to their fellow-members and friends—the sweetest thoughts. Some of the gifts touched us deeply, but owing to the number of presents, and the limited space allowed me, I must leave it to the Hon. Editor's discretion as to which presents call for special mention! The Hon. Editor regrets . . . . . A. S. Lindsey A. S. LINDSEY "Our Dramatic Critic" A. S. LINDSEY A. A. Harley A. A. items.sum: Obituary of W. A. (Bill) Rice, Track Captain and Social Hon. Secretary, who died on 25 April 1936 aged 31.
items.s: Obituary of W. A. (Bill) Rice, Track Captain and Social Hon. Secretary, who died on 25 April 1936 aged 31. It is with the utmost regret, and with a profound sense of our great loss, that we announce the death of our Track Captain, and Social Hon. Secretary, W. A. Rice. Bill had endeared himself to everyone within the Club. For twelve years his influence had been a very real thing to us, and as runner, Committee-man, painstaking Social Hon. Secretary, and diligent Track Captain, he contributed much towards the progress the Club has made during the last decade. Athletics is not merely a matter of championships and performances. It is the means of introducing one to some splendid sportsmen of sterling character, and there are many of us, sorrowful though we may be at the moment, who were glad to have had the privilege of Bill's friendship. His personal qualities meant much to us and the Club he loved, and his memory will be cherished by all who knew him. Bill's thoughts were constantly with the Club throughout his long illness, and his interest was as alive as when he was out and about with us. Even as life ebbed, in his delirious thoughts he lived again his races on the Club's behalf; and, on April 25th, as the Brighton Relay (in which he had captained previous victorious teams) drew to a close, so did our beloved friend's life, at the early age of 31 years. The Club was represented by a dozen or more friends at the funeral, anxious to pay last respects to one who meant so much to all of us. Death has robbed us; but we cannot be robbed of pleasurable memories of a splendid friend, a genial personality, and a hard worker in every phase of the Club's activities. We extend our deepest sympathy to Mrs. Rice, and to the relatives and friends, upon their very great loss. W. A. Rice W. A. Rice Track Captain and Social Hon. Secretary; died 25 April 1936 aged 31; had captained victorious Brighton Relay teams Mrs. Rice Mrs. Rice family of W. A. Rice London to Brighton Relay

items.s: Obituary of young member E. H. M. Williams, a schoolmaster and South of Thames Junior cross-country champion, who died on 25 April 1936 aged 24, with thanks for messages of sympathy. On April 25th also, another young friend, E. H. M. Williams, passed away. His death at the age of 24 years is little short of a tragedy. In his two years of membership, he had established himself as a great favourite with us, and we were all delighted last November when our young schoolmaster friend won the South of Thames C.C. Association's Junior Championship. His running career had seemed full of promise, and his participation in the Club's strolling, social, as well as racing activities, had gained him many friends. We had expected these friendships to last for many years, and the tragic termination of Marshall's life fills us all with very deep regret. It was not possible for the Club to be represented at the funeral, which took place in North Wales; but a floral tribute was sent from the Club. Our profound sympathy goes out to our friend's parents and relatives in their time of sorrow. In his two years with us he had enhanced the Club name, and we have lost another fine personality and splendid clubman. * * * * * We have received several expressions of sympathy from Associations and Clubs, for which we extend our sincere thanks. items.s: THIS AND THAT. Club notes: third successive Brighton Relay win, fifth R.W.A. Junior 10 miles walk team win, Honours Badges for Carter, Churcher and Fletcher, new club ties and track vests, welcoming new members, and a call for field-event athletes. Heartiest congratulations to those responsible for gaining the Club's third successive win in the Brighton Relay—a feat never recorded by any other club. Well done! * * * * * And, well-walked! and more hearty congratulations to the team that won the R.W.A. Junior 10 miles Championship. This is our fifth win—and this again is a feat not yet accomplished by any other club. * * * * * We congratulate C. T. Carter, C. E. Churcher and A. L. Fletcher upon gaining their Club Honours Badges. Carter qualified in the "Southern," Churcher in the "Junior" Walk, and Len Fletcher by gaining first-class standard in the recent A.A.A. 7 miles Championship. His actual position was fourth, and at this meeting Tom Carter ran one of his best races yet in finishing third in the 10 miles Run Championship in very fast time. * * * * * One of the new Club ties at 3/- is just the thing to complete your Summer ensemble, and they may be obtained from the Hon. Treasurer (address on page 1). He will also be glad to receive outstanding subscriptions. * * * * * Within a short time a new sleeveless light-weight vest will be available for track use, and this also may be had from our Hon. Treasurer. * * * * * At this time of the year we are happy to welcome many new members, and they are asked to get in touch with the Club officials as quickly as possible, and make themselves known. Old members, for their part, are asked to do all in their power to advise and help the newcomer. A friendly word and a little practical help are greatly appreciated when one is a newcomer to a sport ; and it is hoped that all members of some years' standing will keep their eyes open for new talent, and assist wherever possible. * * * * * Our Field Events Captain, W. Sutton, would be glad to welcome any athlete interested in Field Events. This section has already made a fine start in the S.A.A.L, competition, which, of course, we won last year. C. T. Carter C. T. e: Belgrave Harriers 10 miles Walk Championship (Murphy Shield)
items.s: THE TEN MILES WALK CHAMPIONSHIP. Report of the club's ten miles walk championship for the Murphy Shield, won by Len Fletcher from Harry Churcher, with Bill Snell and W. Urry taking the handicap awards. The annual contest for the right to hold the "Murphy" Shield for the ensuing year attracted a fair field, including a past holder in Len Fletcher, and the holder, Don Brown. It was soon apparent that Fletcher and Harry Churcher had designs upon the championship, and their rivalry carried them away from the rest of the field; Len winning by a few yards, with the holder filling third position. Bill Snell, who has showed much improved form this year, took the sealed handicap award; and it was pleasing to see a comparative newcomer in W. Urry qualify for the second award. He continues to improve and should help our teams in due course. items.s: THE LONDON TRANSPORT OPEN WALK. Report and results of the London Transport Open Walk at Bellingham, where Belgrave won the scratch team race over Surrey Walking Club and the handicap team award. As usual, our walkers supported the Bellingham Walk in good numbers, and tackled the two-and-a-half laps of hills, gasworks, and housing estate with optimism. Our men were soon prominent, and eventually we had two in the first three places, and our first-choice team scored an easy win over Surrey Walking Club. Three members of the winning scratch team, plus Bill Snell, who took second prize in the handicap, formed the winning handicap team, and altogether we made a most successful visit to Bellingham. items.s: THE ASHCOMBE A.C. OPEN WALK. Report and results of the Ashcombe A.C. Open Walk in Richmond Park, postponed by fog from 15 February to 14 March, where Belgrave's A and B teams took second and third handicap team prizes. This event, fixed for February 15th, had to be postponed owing to dense fog which enveloped the roads in Richmond Park and rendered racing dangerous. Our Ashcombe friends decided to make a second attempt on March 14th, and entries were re-opened. As usual, we had a good muster, and again we supplied two of the first three placed men. There is no scratch team race included in this event (only a set of prizes for the fastest unplaced team in the handicap), and in the handicap team event our Surrey W.C. friends were successful. Our efforts to scheme two teams into placings were successful, the A's taking second place and the B's third prizes. In addition, Bob Readman took third prize in the individual handicap and so brought his tally of awards up to five in four open races. We are expecting big things of him at 10 and 20 miles next season. Pos. Act. Time Allce. H'cap Time 1. G. T. Galloway (S.W.C.) 76 36 1 10 75 26 2. A. L. Fletcher (Bel. A.) 77 9 1 10 75 29 3. D. E. items.label: May 1936
items.sum: T. C. Jones's report and results of the R.W.A. Junior 10 miles walking championship at Colindale on 7 March 1936, in which Belgrave's A team beat Leicester W.C. by 5 points for the club's fifth win in the race, with C. E. Churcher second.
items.s: R.W.A. "JUNIOR" 10 MILES WALKING CHAMPIONSHIP. T. C. Jones's report and results of the R.W.A. Junior 10 miles walking championship at Colindale on 7 March 1936, in which Belgrave's A team beat Leicester W.C. by 5 points for the club's fifth win in the race, with C. E. Churcher second. The "Junior," held on the 7th March from headquarters of the Metropolitan Police A.A. at Colindale, once again saw us win this race, but only after an exciting struggle with Leicester W.C. At about 6½ miles (which was the first time I had been able to see the competitors since the start, and then only after taking a bus ride) Leicester were leading us by 18 points. Staines (Leicester) was leading the field, Charlie Churcher being our first man in 6th position, Percy Wright and Jack Rutland together 10th and 11th, and Charlie Redgrave 26th. Len Storey was leading the "B" team in 27th position, Charlie Speechley 29th (he was "gonged" a little while after this) and C. F. D. Sutton ("B") 33rd. Dunlop W.C. were third with 61 points only 8 points—behind us. Our boys during the next 3 miles put in some fine walking, and when I next checked the scores with about half-a-mile to go, Charlie Churcher had moved up to 2nd place, about 150 yards behind Staines; Percy Wright, 4th; Jack Rutland, 8th; and Charlie Redgrave, 18th. We were only 1 point behind Leicester, with Surrey W.C. now in 3rd place. C. F. D. Sutton was now 26th, leading the "B" team. How well our boys walked in the last half-mile can be gauged from the fact that six points were gained. Charlie Churcher was beaten by only 8 seconds; Percy Wright, 4th; Jack Rutland, 7th; and Charlie Redgrave, 16th; making us winners from Leicester by 5 points. Very appropriate that we should win again in the year of office of Mr. F. G. Thomson as President of the R.W.A.! Our boys were particularly pleased with their win over the most difficult course, for it brought the Club's total of wins in this race to five—a record superior to that of any other club in the country. The hilly nature of the course gave rise to many disqualifications and we suffered in common with other clubs. There is little doubt, however, that we have in our reserve strength a team that will go very near winning again next year. Our "B" team did well to fill 11th position. As a last word, let us pay tribute to gallant losers—Leicester W.C. Nine times out of ten their score is a winning one. This year, second place was their lot. m. s. 1. A. items.s: THE 20 MILES' WALK CHAMPIONSHIP. Report and results of the club 20 miles walk championship, run as a match against a Metropolitan Police W.C. team made up mostly of Belgrave members, won by T. W. Green with Belgrave winning the match 38 points to 40 (the printed handicap positions give 11 to both R. Martin and L. R. Spooner). A match v. Metropolitan Police W.C. was arranged in connection with our Club Championship, their team for this purpose consisting, with one exception, of our own Club members, also in quest of Club honours. All of which sounds rather involved, but actually is very simple, as a glance at the result will show. Our course, which returns almost to the starting point at 8, 11 and 17 miles, once again provided several walkers with an opportunity to "cut it short"—which they accepted. Others kept on...... on...... on...... Tommy Green was the first to reach the finishing post, closely followed by Fred Rickards. Fred, who was winning this race years ago, seems fitter than ever, and we may confidently expect him to demand the attention of the selectors when our Olympic athletes are chosen. It would be a great compliment to our Club and to Police walking if Rickards was chosen, and we know he has the ability and temperament necessary. Third man was Charlie Churcher, a welcome surprise. His first attempt at the distance is full of promise, and he definitely strengthens our team. The next two, Bentley and Bidgood, seemed a little lazy, which means they are saving themselves for future events; and sixth came Bob Readman, who continues to improve and promises to do well. Urry also did well at his first attempt; and in Reeve we have another member who should show up well next season. Churcher's brilliant form earned him first prize in the sealed handicap, with Readman second, and a well-deserving case third. The match v. Police, scoring six aside, gave us a two points win, as the appended result shows. Also started : A. L. Fletcher, W. A. Treacher, R. G. Hillier, B. H. Clark, C. G. Pattenden, G. H. Boddington, F. W. items.s: THE 10 MILES CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Report and results of the club 10 miles cross-country championship, won from the start by Arthur Penny from the holder H. E. Footer, with C. T. Carter first on handicap; 27 finished. A field of 30 faced the starter, Mr. A. E. Macher (Junr.), who paid us one of his infrequent visits to start the race for the Championship for which his father donated the Shield. This was, perhaps, the foundation stone to the present high standard to which our runners have now attained over 10 miles. Previous to the institution of this race, it was very difficult to get the team to train over ten miles, so that when the "Southern" came along our men were always outclassed. The result of the race was never in doubt, barring accidents, as Arthur Penny took the lead from the start, and gradually drew away from the field, eventually winning as he pleased. At the half-distance he was 55 secs. in front of Carter, with Parker next, having a very bad time, and hereabouts he retired. Bert Footer came next. Soon after this, Bert forged ahead to pass Carter, Flower came up from 10th position to 7th to displace Allum, and Shields dropped back a couple of places. These positions were maintained to the finish. 27 finished, which is perhaps the biggest field for a number of years. Although the weather was better than that of last year, there was a slight drizzle of rain and the course was on the heavy side; but this should not have accounted for the race being won in one minute slower time than that of Footer last year. items.label: May 1936
items.sum: G. Doubleday's report and results of the South of the Thames senior cross-country championship at Littlebrook Farm, Dartford, won by F. Close (Reading A.C.), with Belgrave winning the Dewar Shield on 117 points and regaining the Sir J. Colman Cup.
e: South of the Thames Cross Country Championships
items.s: THE SOUTH OF THE THAMES "SENIOR." G. Doubleday's report and results of the South of the Thames senior cross-country championship at Littlebrook Farm, Dartford, won by F. Close (Reading A.C.), with Belgrave winning the Dewar Shield on 117 points and regaining the Sir J. Colman Cup. This race was held from Littlebrook Farm, Dartford, and on the last occasion it was held there Bert Footer was first home. Although most of our "cracks" were barred from this race, we fielded a useful team, our chief rivals being Reading A.C., who included in their team F. Close, the then-reigning National Champion. The sun had thawed the surface of the frost-bound ground, to render it very fast in places. It was a sunny day, although there was a nasty wind blowing. After two laps of the starting field, the runners had strung out. Our Junior Champion, Ted Stimpson, was in the first 10; Alec Patience and Syd Ring were lying handy in the early twenties, with the rest of ours strung out to about the eighties. Two of our men were already in trouble. Marshall Williams found an injured foot a handicap, and Cecil Penny, just after the start, injured one of his legs and seemed to be running with difficulty. After one large lap, our men seemed to be settling down, and after the second, we seemed sure of a place. Stimpson was now 8th, running confidently with speed and style. Micky Walker had come up from the fifties and, running powerfully, overhauled Ring who, handicapped by his light build, experienced difficulties with the wind, and appeared to be losing ground. The last lap began to find some of the competitors out, for the course seemed well over seven miles. F. Close was first home, followed by A. C. Stansbury (Ranelagh). Stimpson sprinted up from 7th to 6th place—a magnificent performance. Patience found his form and improved eleven places on last year's performance, to finish 10th. Walker ran powerfully to be 19th, and Ring split the 3rd and 4th Reading men, to finish 22nd. The position of the teams seemed slightly in favour of Reading, although we both had four men home. But two runners in Claret and Gold appeared in the next group and sprinted round the last bend into the funnel—E. G. Saunders and Frank Webb finished 28th and 32nd, to complete our six. So we won the Championship, scoring 117 pts. to Reading's 153 pts., having picked up 50 places on the last lap. Our next four men—George Chantler, Bert Mitchell, Dave Martin and Bert Jordan—soon closed in. Williams and Penny, who normally would have been battling up the front for a place in the scoring six, ran on pluckily, intent upon finishing, to help the Club to score a double victory by winning the Cup for the lowest score of the complete team of twelve. Both deserved our warm applause for finishing and enabling the Club to regain the "Sir J. Colman" Cup. The "Dewar" Shield for the team championship has only been in our hands once before (1929); but it must be remembered that our Southern and English Championship placings in recent years have barred many of our best runners from participating in this race. Two or three men each year have placed themselves outside the clauses of eligibility laid down in the rules; and made our task of building a winning team in this race more and more difficult. Heartiest congratulations to our winning team of this year for surmounting these difficulties and providing our team selectors with a further set for Season 1936—1937! 1. F. items.label: May 1936
items.sum: Report and results of the Southern Cross-country Championships at Sandown Park, where Ted Stimpson won the Junior race (Belgrave second team; the text says a field of 21 teams, the result 27 teams closed in) and Belgrave were second to Surrey A.C. in the Senior with Tom Carter fifth, winning the Odling-Smee Cup (Surrey A.C.'s printed positions add to 58, printed as 59 pts.).
items.s: THE "SOUTHERN." Report and results of the Southern Cross-country Championships at Sandown Park, where Ted Stimpson won the Junior race (Belgrave second team; the text says a field of 21 teams, the result 27 teams closed in) and Belgrave were second to Surrey A.C. in the Senior with Tom Carter fifth, winning the Odling-Smee Cup (Surrey A.C.'s printed positions add to 58, printed as 59 pts.). This year's Southern Cross-country Championships promised to be among the best ever, and large crowds were expected at Sandown Park. Unfortunately, however, rain intervened, and only the competitors and the real enthusiasts were there to appreciate the organising work which the Committee, under the leadership of this year's President, Mr. W. C. Jewell (who is, of course, a Vice-President of our Club) had done. Proceedings started with the "Junior" race over five miles, and here we were delighted to proclaim one of our runners, Ted Stimpson, as winner. He ran a clever race, using his head as well as his legs, and in perfect style came away in the last mile to win comfortably. Golden opinions were heard everywhere, not only on the achievement, but on the manner of its performance. Unfortunately, George Chantler and Dave Martin were not in their best form; or last year's team win would have been repeated. Lucas, a newcomer, ran well in his first important race in our colours, and clearly has great potentialities. Woodman also did well and, no doubt, his long stride will carry him prominently on the track. Our remaining three juniors never seemed to get going, and show the form we know them to possess. However, it is probably in reserve, for use when they attain senior rank. Our second place in a field of 21 teams must be considered satisfactory, although we were sorry to part with the trophy. The Senior race course extended into the Imber Court district, where plenty of mud was encountered. From the start, Surrey A.C., the holders, were well to the fore and, finding the course to their liking, they proceeded to repeat their last year's win and inflicted a severe defeat upon us. Undoubtedly they were far and away the best team running; and in finishing the first two men home, started off their team scoring in excellent fashion. Of our boys, Tom Carter distinguished himself by finishing fifth, and good packing saw our sixth man finish 24th and our twelfth, 96th. Last year our sixth man was 26th; the previous year, when we won, 27th, so we cannot be said to have gone back. Notable absentees from our team were J. Ginty, A. E. Taylor and D. Patience; but so well did S.A.C. run that it is doubtful whether their presence would have carried us into first place. We were pleased to win, once again, the "Odling-Smee" Cup for the first Surrey club to finish its complete team of twelve. To finish 12 men in the first 96 places in a field of 31 teams is a very creditable performance. m. s. 1. S. C. Belton (S.A.C.) 59 46 5. C. T. Carter 60 22 9. A. W. Penny 60 45 13. H. E. items.label: May 1936
items.sum: Report and results of the English Cross-country Championship at Alderley Edge on 14 March, where Belgrave lost their title to Birchfield Harriers by 22 points, finishing second on 112 points and keeping the Finch Wayte Cup, with Tom Carter qualifying for the International team.
items.s: THE ENGLISH CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP Report and results of the English Cross-country Championship at Alderley Edge on 14 March, where Belgrave lost their title to Birchfield Harriers by 22 points, finishing second on 112 points and keeping the Finch Wayte Cup, with Tom Carter qualifying for the International team. Our team journeyed to Alderley Edge, Cheshire, on March 14th, to defend our title of English Cross-country champions, but Birchfield Harriers carried too many guns for us on this occasion and regained the title. Nevertheless, our team performed very creditably in providing the only real opposition forthcoming to the famous Midland club; and in once again showing that we are the premier Southern Club, by reversing the "Southern" Championship result decided three weeks earlier. Twenty-two points was the margin by which we were beaten; but it must be said that our last year's winning total, although better than this year's, would not have been good enough for first place on this occasion. All of which is a tribute to Birchfield upon the way they have trained to regain their lost title. Well run! And now something of our team and the race itself. Some members of our last year's winning team were not available this time, but we were glad to have Jim Ginty out once again, after his continued ankle trouble. Tom Carter had the distinction of leading our team home, and qualifying for the International team. Arthur Penny and Bert Footer were next home for us, one second separating them; with Jim Ginty close on their heels. Then a gap, and Arthur Allum and Syd Ring completed our scoring team. Our total of 112 points is praiseworthy and once again we hold the "Finch Wayte" Cup for the first Southern club to finish. Next year—the Club's Jubilee Year—should take us into first place again. Although losing the title this year, we were far from disgraced; and we know what has been done once can be repeated! The result is appended. A. R. Shaw (scoring posn. 52), H. W. Shields (54) and A. items.label: May 1936
items.sum: Report and results of the Ilford Relay, where Belgrave's weakened A team finished second to Surrey A.C. and the B team also ran.
items.s: THE ILFORD RELAY. Report and results of the Ilford Relay, where Belgrave's weakened A team finished second to Surrey A.C. and the B team also ran. As last year, we entered two teams in this race, but the result was not so gratifying as then. Owing to last-minute withdrawals, both teams were weakened; the second especially so by having to supply their best men to make up the "A" team. Harry Shields placed us second over the first leg of the race, and then Pat Parker lost a couple of places, only for Bert Shaw to regain them. Alec Patience once again dropped us to fourth place, but Syd Ring brought us up one, and then Jack Flower gave us the lead for the first time. Micky Walker could not however, hold his Surrey A.C. rival, and then George Chantler, Bert Footer, and finally, Arthur Allum, all did their best; but at the finish we were still in second place. Surrey A.C. are to be congratulated on their team's performance. There is no doubt that the best team on the day won, but in view of subsequent events there is some doubt as to whether the final placings will stand. Our "B" team did moderately well and, as some of them were appearing in this class of competition for the first time, I trust they all enjoyed their run and that the experience gained will prove of good value to them in future races. items.label: May 1936
items.sum: Stage-by-stage report of the London to Brighton Relay on 25 April 1936, which Belgrave won for the third successive time, 13 seconds ahead of Birchfield Harriers, with stage results, team placings and a note on the death of C. Young of Queen's Park Harriers.
items.s: THE BRIGHTON RELAY. Stage-by-stage report of the London to Brighton Relay on 25 April 1936, which Belgrave won for the third successive time, 13 seconds ahead of Birchfield Harriers, with stage results, team placings and a note on the death of C. Young of Queen's Park Harriers. April 25th, 1936. The "Bels" made more athletic history by winning this classic race for the third time in succession. Although Birchfield Harriers have had five wins since the race was first inaugurated, we are the first Club to score three wins off the reel. It was perhaps the most thrilling race of the whole series, as only 13 seconds separated the first two teams at the finish. The race this year started from the "News of the World" ground at Mitcham, and the first relay of over 4½ miles was taken by Pat Parker. After a ding-dong struggle he handed over to Harry Shields, with a lead of 14 seconds. A hard fight took place in the next stage of about 5½ miles, and eventually Harry finished two seconds behind the Herne Hill Harrier, P. Hennessey, who only a few days previously had won the Inter-Services Cross-Country Championship. In the next relay of about 4¾ miles, Jack Webster came in for Birchfield; and showing some of his old form, he ran splendidly in putting his team 28 seconds in front of Jack Flower at the take-over. Syd Ring took the next stage of just over 4¾ miles to Buckland, and running with very sound judgment, just managed to get in front by one second. Arthur Penny now took up the running and had a tussle to shake off the Birchfield international, A. Bourton, but running very strongly he handed over to Bert Shaw, with 17 secs. in hand. Another titanic struggle took place in this next relay of about 5½ miles to Crawley, and eventually Shaw handed over 6 seconds behind his Birchfield rival. Ted Stimpson, our Southern Junior C.C. Champion, had been entrusted with the next stage of about 4½ miles to Handcross; but was unable to make any headway against his more experienced rival, and eventually handed over to Tom Carter with a deficit of 30 seconds. Carter set about his task in a workmanlike manner and, running in beautiful style, soon had the measure of his opponent, and overhauling him, Tom then proceeded to open as large a gap as was humanly possible. When he handed over at Hickstead to Bert Footer, we had a lead of 11 seconds, which at this point was invaluable. The ninth stage has always been Bert's favourite. Incidentally, it is reckoned the toughest of the lot, being a long, steady climb all the way; and although his Birchfield opponent ran very strongly, Bert increased our advantage to 20 seconds. Arthur Allum, as last year, had been allotted the final stage to Brighton; and although chased by the Scottish International, R. R. Sutherland, he grimly held on to the lead to finish first, 13 seconds in front. So we scored a wonderful victory, in which all our team played their part in fine style. In a race of this description it is almost useless to put one performance above another; a few seconds gained on one stage may be just as valuable as a larger margin on another. Special mention might be made, however, of Pat Parker, who fully justified our hopes of him; Tom Carter, who, although faced with the task of tackling an opponent who was out of sight when he commenced his stage, yet reeled off mile after mile in automatic fashion. He not only caught his rival, but gave us a lead, which at this stage was the real turning point of the race. Arthur Allum ran in his own indomitable fashion, and when you consider Sutherland's performances this season, to gain only 7 seconds on our man over a distance of 6½ miles was a distinct feather in Arthur's cap. We were all very deeply shocked to hear of the death of C. Young, of Queen's Park Harriers, who was knocked down by a motor-car and died on his way to hospital. A letter of sympathy has been sent to his club. The new course was, to my mind, not so open as the old Brighton Road, and on some of the stages the congestion was intense. The chief cause of this appeared to be the number of small private cars which would persist in keeping near the runner, instead of pushing forward to the next take-over, and awaiting him there. We had our usual two buses following the race, but as one of these was carrying our runners it was imperative that we got to the next stage in the quickest possible time, and therefore no charge can be levelled at us for causing any delay. Whether this race will continue on the present lines is in the lap of the gods, but it does seem that the time has come to limit the number of teams competing, and by so doing correspondingly reduce the number of followers to the race. items.s: THE FIVE MILES ROAD HANDICAP. Report and result of the club's Five Miles Road Handicap on 4 April 1936, won on actual time by Allum and on handicap by White; three printed handicap times do not agree with actual time less allowance. April 4th was the revised date for this fixture, which usually throws light upon our Brighton Relay prospects, and helps when our team selection is considered. Allum was soon to the front, with Parker in close attendance, and this remained the position until a mile to go. Then a leg injury of Parker's asserted itself, and he began to drop places sensationally. Meanwhile, Footer was coming through the field at great speed, and eventually finished second, only two seconds behind Allum. Shields did well to finish third, and among the others, Ted Stimpson was generally thought to have done well. It was pleasing to see several comparative newcomers showing fair form, which should in due course find them places in our teams. RESULT. Act. Time Allce. H'cap Time H'cap Posn. 1. items.label: May 1936
items.sum: Notice to members of the 1936 summer handicap meetings at Battersea Park, with novice races, the entry fee and a new rule that only entrants printed on the programme may compete.
items.s: HANDICAPS. Notice to members of the 1936 summer handicap meetings at Battersea Park, with novice races, the entry fee and a new rule that only entrants printed on the programme may compete. Just a few lines addressed to members both old and new. As you will see from your Summer fixture card, we have Handicaps at our meetings in Battersea Park on the following dates :— May 20th (Wed.)—220 Yards for members under 19 years of age. 880 Yards. 2 Miles Walk. Javelin Throw. June 3rd (Wed.)—100 Yards. 1 Mile Run. 2 Miles Walk. 120 Yards Hurdles (the Hurdles will be 3ft. in order to encourage entries). Also on this evening we are holding two Novice races. One is a 100 Yards and the other a 1 Mile Walk. These are level events open to ALL Unattached Novices, that is those who do not belong to any other athletic club and have not won a prize since leaving school. If you have any young friends, get them interested; entry is FREE and medals will be awarded to the first three in each race. June 17th (Wed.)—Shot Putt. (This is the night of the Inter-Club Walks; so we trust our Weight(y) men will not maim any of the competitors). June 24th (Wed.)—100 Yards. 1 Mile Run. 2 Miles Walk. (These are open to members of the competing clubs for the "Doris" Shield). Long Jump (open to Belgrave members only). July 15th (Wed.)—100 Yards for our young lads under 16 years of age. 220 Yards. 880 Yards. 100 Yards for our Veteran members over 40 years of age. 2 Miles Walk. High Jump. In addition we have a 1 Mile run open to Unattached Novices, and this will be on the same lines as the two preceding events of the same class. August 19th (Wed.)—100 Yards. 440 Yards. 1 Mile Run. 2 Miles Walk. Shot Putt. September 5th (Sat).—100 Yards. 880 Yards. Long Jump. In case any of you have carefully checked up on last year's card, let me say, here and now, that there are two fewer handicaps this year. One is a 220 Yards, the other the 2 Miles run. The fixtures for this season were very carefully considered, and I am sure you will not cavil at the result of our efforts. The entries last year were hardly up to standard, and although we can never hope to cover ourselves as regards the financial side of these events, we do at least expect better support, and so make us think our efforts on your behalf have been worth while. To new members I would say, if you aspire to a place in our club teams, then your surest way is through the medium of club handicaps. The marks are always fairly given in accordance with what is known of a members' ability, and success here would quickly put you in the team selectors' eyes. The fee for all club events is 1/-, and entries should be either handed in at Battersea Park to the responsible club official, or be posted direct to the Club Handicapper. In order to avoid any last-minute rush, entries sent in at least 7 days before the meeting will be much appreciated. In the past many members have been allowed to compete although their names have not appeared on the programme. It is always hard for us club officials to turn down good money, but in fairness to the rest of the competitors who have had the good grace to enter beforehand, the Committee have decided that only those whose names appear in print will be allowed to compete. So to those of you who may have been guilty of such lapses in the past, take heed lest your chance of winning a prize vanishes in the vision of the card that you meant to write, but didn't ! Inter-Club Walks Doris Shield Battersea Park

items.label: May 1936
items.sum: Preview of Belgrave's 1936 summer track fixtures, from the Inter-Club Relay Shield and Doris Shield to Club Championship Day, ahead of the Berlin Olympic Games, with a tribute to the late Bill Rice.
items.s: NON-STOP TO BERLIN ! Preview of Belgrave's 1936 summer track fixtures, from the Inter-Club Relay Shield and Doris Shield to Club Championship Day, ahead of the Berlin Olympic Games, with a tribute to the late Bill Rice. We now commence another Track season; and for some of our members I hope it will prove their best ever, and that they will have the great honour of wearing Britain's vest at the 1936 Olympiad. As these notes are now published quarterly, I don't propose to waste your eyesight by making you read through date after date of our Summer Fixture card. Every member should have received one of these, and so I will confine myself to just mentioning a few of the more important fixtures. On May 20th we have an evening meeting at Battersea Park Track. All our evening meetings at this venue will be held on Wednesdays and will start at 7 p.m. prompt. On this date the first of the Inter-Club Relay Shield competitions will be decided. The events take the form of relays, viz., 4 x 100 Yards, 4 x 300 Yards, 4 x 880 Yards and a 1 Mile Team race in which 4 men run for each club and all score. The present holders of the Shield are Mitcham A.C., and unless our members make a determined effort to turn up at the away matches, I can foresee no change in the ownership of the Shield. Harry Shields is our new Track Captain and if only you will support him the same way as some of you used to do Bill Rice, I am sure Harry will think that he is filling Bill's shoes in a manner worthy of his predecessor. In Bill Rice you had an athlete who virtually lived for his running, and, what was more important, at least to him, his club. If you want to honour his memory I know of no better way than by regaining this Inter-Club Relay Shield, for which Bill had run some of the hardest races of his life. On June 2nd we have a Junior (under 19) contest versus Croydon H., Mitcham A.C. and Epsom H. (which will be held on the former's ground), with the following events : 3 x 100 Yards, 3 x 200 Yards, and 880 Yards Team race with 4 to run, 3 to score. Will all those members who are eligible to compete kindly get in touch with me, in order to select our team? The following evening, June 3rd, at Battersea Park, we have a match with Leigh-on-Sea H., and Imperial College A.C. This should give a chance to those members who could not compete on the previous evening. On June 9th is the second of the series of contests for the Inter-Club Relay Shield, this time on Croydon Harriers' new ground at Plough Lane, Beddington. This is quite near West Croydon, in case some of you Londoners don't know your way about ! On June 24th, at Battersea Park, we are holding the Doris Shield contest, and our opponents for this trophy will be Thames Valley H. and Ashcombe A.C. All the events are level races, viz., 100 Yards, 440 Yards, 2 Miles Team race and a 1 Mile Medley Relay. There will be the usual Handicaps, open to all members of the three competing clubs. On Saturday, June 27th, we have a match with that very promising club, the Southgate Harriers. They are building on very sound foundations, and I am sure our lads will find foemen worthy of their steel (I must have been seeing "The Three Musketeers" !) when they visit Broomfield Park. On July 2nd, at Kingston, we tread new ground by visiting the Old Tiffinians A.C. for a series of match events. Those of you who remember our pleasant little fixtures with the Old Gaytonians and Emanuel School will appreciate the chance that such matches as these give to some of our younger members. On July 15th, at Battersea Park, we have a triangular contest with the Polytechnic Harriers and Victoria Park H. The latter club are new to our fixture list, but I can assure you that in my capacity as an A.A.A. Handicapper, I have a very healthy respect for their members' abilities on the running track. On July 22nd we are at Deptford Park, and our opponents will be Herne Hill H. and Blackheath H. Quite a stiff little problem to overcome, but so long as our members turn up—well ! personally, I don't care which way the result goes ! I leave it to the boys ! Saturday, July 25th, is Club Championship Day, and we start at 3 p.m. at Battersea Park Track. There are championships at all distances and with the 440 yards and upwards we give standard medals, and I can assure you the standards we have set are within the reach of all members who have trained conscientiously throughout the season. A new feature of our meeting will be the deciding of five Field Event Championships and I trust they will be well supported and so repay the efforts of George Powell and Bill Sutton, who have done so much in securing the awarding of these championships. On July 29th we have the third Inter-Club Relay contest, at the "News of the World" Sports Ground, Mitcham. I hope we shall have a good following present, as this is always a most exciting meeting and, moreover, the proceeds all go towards a very deserving cause. And so to Berlin for the Games, August 1st to 9th ! The rest our our summer fixtures will be dealt with in our next issue of the "Belgravian." All entries and enquiries to— E. A. DUFFETT, Asst. Hon. Sec., 10, Barrow Road, Waddon, Croydon. items.sum: Walking-section notes for summer 1936: entry rules, the Kinnaird Meeting team walk, the Inter-club Walks, and hopes of a third 50 kilos team title with Olympic possibilities Green, Rickards and Bentley.
items.s: WITH THE WALKERS. Walking-section notes for summer 1936: entry rules, the Kinnaird Meeting team walk, the Inter-club Walks, and hopes of a third 50 kilos team title with Olympic possibilities Green, Rickards and Bentley. Another track season is with us, and by now you all have the Summer fixture list, giving all the dates of Club Hndicaps and Championships. Members are reminded that only those whose names appear on the programme will be allowed to compete this season, and so all entries should be sent to the Walk. Hon. Secretary or Walk. Hon. Handicapper. seven days in advance. * * * * * We have accepted an invitation to compete in a Two Miles Team Walk at the Kinnaird Meeting at the White City, on June 13th. We should have a useful team for this fixture. * * * * * The Annual Inter-club Walks will take place at Battersea Park on Wednesday, June 17th, when we expect to receive the usual splendid support from the Metropolitan Clubs. This is always a big date in the walkers' calendar. * * * * * The 50 kilos Walk Championship, which has added significance this year in view of the Olympic Games, will be held on July 4th, probably at Derby. We have held the team title for the last two years; and with Green, Rickards and Bentley, all Olympic possibilities, supported by others, we should claim a "hat trick." Best of luck to our men in their quest for Olympic honours ! * * * * * We are always glad to welcome new men to our ranks, and it is hoped that all walkers will see if it is not possible to introduce a friend to the sport. The more the merrier. New members quickly become old friends ! * * * * * All entries and enquiries to A. A. HARLEY, 39, Roxborough Avenue, Isleworth, Mx. items.label: August 1936
items.sum: Editorial notes: Jim Ginty's Olympic selection, protest at Fred Bentley's omission from the Olympic walking team, the R.W.A. 50 kilos. team win, members' marriages and deaths, club tie and vests, marathon standard medals, a letter from A. F. Mitchell and the editor's look back at his first issue of 1929.
items.s: THIS AND THAT. Editorial notes: Jim Ginty's Olympic selection, protest at Fred Bentley's omission from the Olympic walking team, the R.W.A. 50 kilos. team win, members' marriages and deaths, club tie and vests, marathon standard medals, a letter from A. F. Mitchell and the editor's look back at his first issue of 1929. Twelve months ago these columns recorded our indignation at the non-selection of Jim Ginty as a member of the English International team, after he had so clearly demonstrated his claims in the A.A.A. Championships. Now it gives us all the greatest of pleasure to congratulate Jim upon his inclusion in the British Olympic team. We are sure he will acquit himself well, and expect him to reach the final of the Steeplechase, and uphold the prestige of his Country and Club. Our best wishes go with Jim! * * * * * In the midst of our pleasure at this selection, it is unfortunate that we should have to express our disappointment that Fred Bentley, who finished third in the recent R.W.A. 50 kilos. Championship, has not been asked to accompany the team. Many of us think he was entitled to his place in the trio to represent Gt. Britain; and it is certain that his fairness, combined with speed and stamina, would have ensured a creditable performance. However, we are not prepared to criticise too harshly the selection of the three to travel. Whitlock and Hopkins made clear their claims beyond any shadow of doubt, and T. Lloyd Johnson, although failing on this occasion, has sterling performances to his credit in the past. We wish them the best of luck, and feel certain that England's walkers will be very prominent. Our great disappointment is that Fred Bentley should be denied the honour of being nominated as first reserve. We are unable to trace the slightest degree of justification for this omission. Our man's previous performances, and placing in the official Olympic trial, cry out for recognition. And that recognition appears to have been granted by everyone except the Selection Committee! To those of us familiar with past and present form at the Olympic distance, the reserve selection came as a tremendous surprise; for both Bentley and Green possessed greater claims for nomination on current form and past experience. Protests on the journey homewards from Derby were successful in obtaining a slight concession to reasonableness, and it was agreed that Bentley's name should go forward to the International Board as a further reserve. * * * * * It is our Committee's intention to pursue this matter further, as was done in the case of Ginty last year, in an attempt to gain some slight redress; and to protect the interests of others who in future years may find themselves similarly treated, if no protest is made on this occasion. Fortunately, Fred Bentley has a big heart and youth on his side, and there is every probability that International honours may come to him later, as they have done to Jim Ginty. * * * * * The Metropolitan Police Walking Club, among whom we have so many loyal members, have shared our disgust at Bentley's rejection (he is Police Champion over the Southend—Barking course), and have given us their whole-hearted support. Whether any satisfaction, or mitigation of this recent action, can be forthcoming is problematical, but it is certain that an investigation, when called for by two large representative bodies such as the M.P.W.C. and ourselves, and backed by an imposing array of incontrovertible facts, must take place and, we trust, ensure future selection is of a more logical character. Only by a strict inquiry, and the amende honorable, can the Road Walking Association regain some of the confidence it has recently forfeited. * * * * * And now, heartiest congratulations to our team that won the National Team Championship (which carries with it the handsome "Horlick" Cup), in the R.W.A. 50 kilos. Championship at Derby. This is our third successive win, and the same three men (Fred Bentley, Tommy Green and Fred Rickards) have constituted the team on each occasion, but they have contrived to finish in a different order each time. Well walked! Our very best wishes for future happiness go to L. F. Bailey, D. E. Brown and B. J. T. Knifton upon the occasion of their respective marriages. The last two named, in particular, have done much for the Club, and to all three we send our congratulations and good wishes. * * * * * In our last issue we had the sad duty of recording the passing of two good friends. Again, we have to announce the loss of another two loyal Belgravians. Capt. W. H. Ellison, a Vice-President for some years past, and a familiar figure at Wimbledon throughout the winter months, and G. H. Laurie, a regular participant in the London—Brighton Walk, have both passed over. We feel this added loss acutely, and tender our sincere sympathy to the relatives concerned. * * * * * The new Club tie, with the badge woven in gold on a claret background, is now available, and application should be made to the Hon. Treasurer. The price is 3/-. * * * * * Several members are making the trip to see the Olympic Games, and no doubt hundreds will be in attendance at the British Empire v. U.S.A. match at the White City, on August 15th. * * * * * A note from our Track Captain, Harry Shields, comes as a reminder that light-weight sleeveless Club vests may now be had from the Hon. Treasurer, at 2/6 each. There can now be no possible excuse for members not wearing the Club vest; and those erring souls who have been seen at meetings, hiding themselves beneath the anonymity of a white vest, are invited, to send their chest measurements and half-a-crown to Mr. W. G. Webb at once. * * * * * Our Track Captain, in collaboration with E. Stimpson, also has ideas about the formation of a subscription club to purchase training suits. The price is expected to be in neighbourhood of 15/- to 17/6, and those interested are invited to get into touch with either of the above-named. But get that Club vest first! * * * * * Congratulations to A. F. Mitchell and F. A. Walker upon their recent Marathon performance—a distance which has been neglected in recent years by our members. Both men qualified for Polytechnic H. standard medals in the Kinnaird Marathon, and followed this up by gaining A.A.A. standard medals on July 11th, and so, by complying with the condition laid down, qualified for their Club Honours Badges. In this latter race, our two men finished together, their time being just outside 2 hours 52 minutes for the 26 miles 385 yards journey—very fine performances. * * * * * In this connection we have pleasure in publishing the following letter received :— Dear Mr Harley, I should be glad if through the pages of the Magazine you would allow me to express my thanks for the kindness shown by Messrs. Frank Elson and Percy Wright during the Marathon races. Their encouragement was greatly appreciated. Yours faithfully, (Signed) A. F. MITCHELL. * * * * * Our last issue of "The Belgravian" was the fiftieth to see the light since I succeeded Ben Knifton as Hon. Editor of our Gazette in April, 1929, and this fact sent me foraging into the first issue I timorously presented to our members It is interesting to see there recorded the plans for the formation of the Southern Amateur Athletic League, which we now accept as part of the normal Summer programme. Also an account of the National Cross-country Championship at Beaconsfield, when we started eight men, and finished only four. The heroes of this intensely hot day were : W. G. Webb (87th), A. W. Penny (120th), W. L. Bayliss (122nd) and F. G. Ford (197th). We also recorded in this issue the winning of an open team track race—the second occasion ever to do so, at that time; and concluded the Gazette with words that have not yet lost their point, as follows :— "To conclude, constructive criticism, helpful suggestions, in fact, anything which tends to improve our magazine and raise it to a higher level, will be gratefully received. The publication of a Club magazine calls for more team work than the winning of a championship, and your help will be welcomed as a personal favour by THE HON. EDITOR." items.label: August 1936
items.sum: Announcement that the Club is about to take the lease of St. John's Hall, Wimbledon, as headquarters, with an appeal for the Building Fund.
items.s: OUR WIMBLEDON HEADQUARTERS. Announcement that the Club is about to take the lease of St. John's Hall, Wimbledon, as headquarters, with an appeal for the Building Fund. As we go to press, arrangements have almost been completed for the acquisition of the lease of St. John's Hall, Wimbledon. The Committee have given this matter their most careful consideration, and it has been decided to take advantage of the opportunity which has presented itself; and so we can be sure of quarters within easy reach of our Wimbledon Common and Richmond Park training grounds for at least another twenty years. It is hoped to add to the amenities of the Hall—which has, of course, been impossible in the past—and generally equip it so that we shall have a first-class athletic and social centre for years to come. Our Committee are likely to have some late nights planning any alterations and developments that may be decided upon, and the co-operation of all members will be needed to ensure that Belgrave Hall (or whatever we decide to call our headquarters) is the success it deserves to be. And so the present needs of the Club have, to some extent, at least, been satisfied, and pleasingly enough, satisfied now, so that those who have worked and contributed to our Building Fund can share some of the benefits that ownership of our own quarters can offer, rather than that posterity alone should benefit. The need for our Building Fund is, of course, more important now than ever before. The initial cost, possible alterations, equipment and maintenance have to be met, and additionally, we shall still strive to raise enough money to ensure quarters—eventually—in perpetuity for the Club. This has always been one of our aims, and remains so; even while we consider and cater for immediate needs. We are sure that this announcement will give general pleasure to those who have enjoyed past Winter seasons at Wimbledon; and we hope that more than ever will be present on our opening day and subsequent Saturdays throughout the season. Details of the early Winter fixtures will be given in the Annual General Meeting notice, when it is circulated. St. John's Hall, Wimbledon Wimbledon Common Richmond Park

items.s: THE R.W.A. 20 MILES NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP. Report and result of the R.W.A. 20 miles National Championship at Leicester on May 9th, where Belgrave were third team, one point behind Leicester W.C., and the Surrey Walking Club won for the fourth successive time; the printed Belgrave scorers' positions (5, 8, 17, 27) add to 57, not the 53 points shown. The "Senior" Championship was held on May 9th at Leicester, and we set off from London feeling that we were sure of our usual placing, and had a good chance of upsetting the Surrey Walking Club's series of wins. We knew that on current form our complete team of eight were not so good as those of our rivals, but from positions 1—5, as shown in our Club Championship, we thought we were slightly superior. Unfortunately, our margin of safety was insufficient. Charlie Churcher had the misfortune to suffer disqualification early on; and Tommy Green, although prominent in the first half of the race, was troubled by cramp in the tops of the legs towards the end, and gradually dropped back. Meanwhile, Fred Rickards and Fred Bentley were giving us their usual sound performances, and Jack Bidgood, after a quiet start, began to peg back places. With the slowing of Green, our need for a fourth man became apparent, and here Bob Readman came into prominence and completed our team. This was his first "National 20," and reflects the greatest credit on him. Next year he should knock several minutes off his time and step into the very front rank of 20-mile walkers. With the withdrawal of Churcher and the indisposition of Green, our hopes of winning had long since gone, but we still seemed set for second place. In the last few yards, however, Lloyd Johnson managed to pass Fred Rickards and so took his club into second position, and relegated us to third place, one point separating us. Of our non-scoring "A" team men, Green gained a first-class standard medal, and Harley and Urry second-class medals. Our "B" team acquitted themselves well in finishing 12th of the 17 teams to close in. This is very creditable, and we expect further improvement from them next year. B. H. Clark, S. Goold and G. H. Boddington of this team gained second-class standard awards. The Surrey Walking Club were responsible for a very fine show in scoring their fourth successive win, and we proffer our heartiest congratulations. They, too, had their misfortunes in the disqualification of Archibald and the falling-back of Galloway, but superior reserve strength enabled them to survive. As pointed out earlier, our margin of safety was not so good, and we must concentrate on this next year. The result is appended. RESULT. 126 finished. TEAM PLACINGS. 17 teams closed in. Pos. items.label: August 1936
items.sum: Report of the R.W.A. 50 kilos. Championship at Derby on July 4th, where Belgrave won the team championship and the "Horlick" Cup for the third successive year, Fred Bentley finishing third inside the previous best figures.
items.s: THE R.W.A. 50 KILOS. CHAMPIONSHIP. Report of the R.W.A. 50 kilos. Championship at Derby on July 4th, where Belgrave won the team championship and the "Horlick" Cup for the third successive year, Fred Bentley finishing third inside the previous best figures. This Team Championship, carrying with it the "Horlick" Cup, is ours again for the third successive year. From the start at Derby on July 4th, our men were always prominent and there never seemed any possibility of our having to hand over the trophy. Fred Bentley, in particular, excelled himself, and was with the leaders up to 28 miles, when they managed to drop him, but he carried through and recorded the splendid timing given below. The previous best figures for this Championship were 4 hr. 35 min. 36 sec. by Tommy Green at Croydon in 1930. Fred was over two minutes better than this, and yet was only third. This truly fine performance of Fred's earned him many congratulations immediately after the race. The disappointment which took away the gloss came later; but we have expressed our views of this on another page. Our next man to finish was Tommy Green, in fourth position. Tommy took some time to settle down, but towards the end he was his old self. In fact, his time from the 25 miles mark to the finish (just over 6 miles) was faster than that of any other man in the race. Even Whitlock was 17 seconds slower; all of which shows that Tommy is very far from being the spent force some people would like us to believe. Our team was completed by Fred Rickards in sixth position. One could not help but feel sorry for Fred. He looked as fit as he has ever done. Special training had put him into the pink of condition, and yet on the day of days he had the misfortune to have stomach troubles, which lost him many minutes. But for this, it is certain that Fred would have been right in the front, and qualified for an Olympic position. However, Fred has learned some philosophy in the course of many years' walking, and met misfortune with a smile. A week later he walked Lloyd Johnson to a yard in 25 miles, both men being well inside previous record! Such is the luck of the game. Our other man to finish was Jack Bidgood. He was always there should any of our first three be forced to retire, and qualified for a first-class standard medal. Well walked, Jack! Our congratulations go to Harold Whitlock upon his exceptionally fine walking, and to J. Hopkins, who made sure of a place in the Olympic team. We should not be surprised to see them finish first and second at Berlin. RESULT. 30 finished. TEAM PLACINGS. Pos. Name h. m. s. 1. H. H. Whitlock (Met. W.C.) 4 30 38 2. J. Hopkins (Lancs. items.sum: Report of the inter-club scratch walks at Battersea Park on June 17th over 1, 2, 3 and 5 miles, won by Belgrave with 110 points from Surrey Walking Club and Metropolitan W.C., with Harry Churcher winning the two miles and Don Brown the one mile.
items.s: THE INTER-CLUB WALKS. Report of the inter-club scratch walks at Battersea Park on June 17th over 1, 2, 3 and 5 miles, won by Belgrave with 110 points from Surrey Walking Club and Metropolitan W.C., with Harry Churcher winning the two miles and Don Brown the one mile. Our annual programme of scratch walks at 1, 2, 3 and 5 miles once again received good support from the Metropolitan clubs when the events took place at Battersea Park on June 17th. Woodford Green A.C. were unable to accept an invitation this year owing to other arrangements, but next year we hope to welcome them again. The competition was on the usual lines, two men from each club competing in each event where possible (no man walking twice during the evening), and 16 points were allocated to the Club providing the winner, 15 points to the second man's club, and so on downwards. The aggregate of points on the evening gave us a win with 110 points, to the 100 of Surrey Walking Club, and 79 of the Metropolitan W.C. The first race to be held was the Five Miles Walk, and in this Harold Whitlock (Met. W.C.) gave a splendid exhibition, finishing an easy winner in 38 min. 16 sec. Burt (S.W.C.) was second, Len Fletcher, of ours, third. Our other man, Fred Bentley, found the distance a bit too short for his liking, but did well to finish fifth. The scoring by the clubs was Belgrave and S.W.C. each 26 points, Metropolitan W.C. 25 points. RESULT. 1, H. Whitlock (Met. W.C.), 38m. 16s.; 2, N. Burt (S.W.C.), 39m. 6s.; 3, A. L.
