items.sum: Walking notes: a good start to the winter season, prospects for the 'Junior' Championship team, Continental results from F. G. Thomson, the Club Open 7 Miles Walk and French match at Wimbledon, and future walking fixtures.
items.s: With the Walkers. Walking notes: a good start to the winter season, prospects for the 'Junior' Championship team, Continental results from F. G. Thomson, the Club Open 7 Miles Walk and French match at Wimbledon, and future walking fixtures. Another Winter season is here, and we have made a good start. With a Brighton team walk win, recently recorded, an easy win in our first inter-club match of the season, and a whole heap of success in the first "Open" of the year, we can feel satisfied. We have had some splendid scratch teams at seven and ten miles in the past, but this year's team personnel seems to be well up to previous standards. A continuance of the excellent form shown so early in the season should ensure many more successes in the months before us. * * * * * We are glad to welcome several new members to our ranks. Several have already shown up well in racing, and there are others likely to develop into first-class walkers in the near future. * * * * * Our "Junior" team for the Championship next March will quite likely be the strongest we have ever fielded—and that is indeed saying something. The Club's low record of 26 points in 1933, when H. G. Churcher, D. E. Brown, A. H. Field and A. A. Harley formed our team, stands a good chance of being beaten, so strong does our team appear. The Championship is still several months away but carefully balanced training and racing during the intervening period should give us a very fit team. Of the constitution of the team it would be, perhaps, a little too early to write now, for there are many with claims. All being well, another issue of the "Belgravian" should appear next February, and we may be able to indulge in a little prophecy then. * * * * * We are indebted to Mr. F. G. Thomson for a summary of the principal walking results from abroad. Unfortunately, pressure on our columns does not permit us to reproduce these results in full; but it is very evident that road-walking is progressing at a great rate on the Continent. Details are given of racing in France, Germany, Norway, Denmark, Holland, Latvia, Italy, Sweden and even Abyssinia. Familiar names to appear include Laisné (France), Schwab (Germany), Dalinsch (Latvia) and Mikaelson (Sweden). The standard appears to be very high, and we look forward to the time when international team walks are an accepted part of our programme. The difficulties, of course, are many; but difficulties were made to be overcome, and we trust the R.W.A. and A.A.A. will be able to make some progress in this direction. * * * * * The Club Open 7 Miles Walk takes place on Saturday, November 27th, at Wimbledon. As usual, all our active Club walkers are expected to support our promotion, and it would be very helpful if entry forms were sent in well before the official closing date. We expect the usual excellent support from other Clubs; and an extra attraction this year will be the stern competition for the "Berman" Cup, allocated by the R.W.A. to our race, to be held by the winners of the scratch team race. We trust all those not actively participating will come along to Wimbledon on November 27th as spectators. * * * * * December 11th is the day when we expect foreign opposition at Wimbledon. To give all our walkers a chance to turn out against our French friends, all our members will be eligible to compete and a sealed handicap will be held in conjunction, embracing all Club members. Additionally, the Club Junior Championship for the "Horwood Cup" will be held in conjunction with the match. All first-claim members having a "Junior" qualification according to R.W.A. rules can compete for the "Horwood" Cup, which is held at present by C. Speechley. * * * * * Future fixtures are:— Nov. 13—Enfield A.C. Open Walk at Enfield. Nov. 27—Belgrave H. Open Walk at Wimbledon. Dec. 11—Match v. l'Union Sportive Metropolitaine, with sealed handicap and Club "Junior" Championship ("Horwood" Cup). Dec. 27 (Boxing Day)—Croydon-Godstone and Back Open Walk (18¾ miles). items.sum: Report and result of the club's Five Miles Walk Handicap at Wimbledon on 2 October 1937, won by R. F. Elson from J. A. Bellchambers; three printed handicap times (Bridger, L. J. Coleman, Jarvis) do not match actual time minus allowance.
items.s: The Five Miles Walk Handicap. Report and result of the club's Five Miles Walk Handicap at Wimbledon on 2 October 1937, won by R. F. Elson from J. A. Bellchambers; three printed handicap times (Bridger, L. J. Coleman, Jarvis) do not match actual time minus allowance. An entry of 25 for our first handicap of the Winter season on October 2nd was very gratifying, and seems to indicate a good season ahead. In this race the man with the greatest allowance starts away first, and this was the privilege of G. S. Doubleday. He has been known as a runner in the the past, but it is certain that in a few months' time we shall look upon him as one of our future "Junior" team men. He was closely followed by two other newcomers of undoubted promise in A. E. Elliott and J. Ogilvie. In a short time all the walkers were in action, and the results of our Hon. Handicapper's deliberations were awaited with interest. It was soon obvious that Tony Bellchambers and Reg Elson, who started off together, would set a very hot pace. So hot was it that nobody else could catch them, and Elson, with his extra years and experience, managed to draw away from his younger rival in the closing stages. Both walked very well, as did also Bob Martin, who took third prize. Among the entrants were R. Stevens, A. H. Bridger, and H. Thaxter, in addition to those already mentioned, racing for the first time at Wimbledon in a club race; and all showed they will be valuable in their assistance to our teams. The race must be considered one of the most successful yet held, and the form displayed gives us hope of a record season. Our usual team men seem to be shaping up well, and among the newcomers there is much talent only requiring the necessary training and perseverance to enable them to become first team men in their turn. items.s: Highgate Harriers' Open Walk. Report and results of the Highgate Harriers' Open Walk, won by Harry Churcher, with Belgrave winning the scratch and handicap team races; J G Coleman's printed handicap time does not match actual time minus allowance. "Belgrave Well off the Mark." "Clean Sweep in Highgate Open." These headings taken from "The Sporting Life" indicate that we had little to complain of at the first open walk of the season. Eighteen of our walkers entered, comprising two teams—the largest entry from any club. All started, and claret and gold vests were soon prominent at the head of the field. Harry Churcher eventually had an easy win from F. J. Redman, and V. W. Stone. Our supporting men were always well placed, and at the finish we had our fourth man in actual 10th position. We had six in 14 positions; and seven "A" team in the first 18 places. Naturally such splendid walking gained an easy team win for the Club, and our "A" team were also successful in the handicap team event. In this the "B" team were placed third. Thus nine "firsts" went to the Club and four "thirds," and Len Coleman took the special prize for the member of the Club with largest entry, not gaining any other award. So Belgrave had 14 prizes out of 23! The individual handicap winner, H. G. Clayton (6m. 30s.) actually finished fifth in the scratch race, and held a special interest for us as he has been advised and encouraged by Tommy Green. He is now a Belgrave Harrier. e: Belgrave Harriers v. Metropolitan Police walking match
items.s: At Imber Court. Report and result of the seven-mile walking match v. Metropolitan Police at Imber Court, won easily by Belgrave, 140 pts. to 221; dated November 16th in an issue labelled November 1937. On November 16th, our walkers visited Imber Court for a match v. Metropolitan Police, and, as usual, found among our rivals many who are usually our team-mates. Thirteen aside were the numbers decided upon for scoring purposes, and away went 40 walkers over the usual flat seven miles course. Before a mile had been covered, our men were well placed, and as the race progressed so did our lead over our Police rivals. We had the satisfaction of finishing the first seven men, and ten in the first thirteen placings. This gave us our easiest win for many years. In fact, in recent years we have often been narrowly beaten, the strength of the Police in the middle section of the race usually being the deciding factor. It is worthy of note that 15 of the first 19 to finish are Belgrave Harriers. It is always pleasant to visit the very sporting Police team at their Imber Court quarters, and we may be well sure that they will be all out to reverse their defeat when they visit us at Wimbledon in January. m. s. 1. items.s: Club 3 Miles Road Race. Report and full handicap result of the Club 3 Miles Road Race at Wimbledon on Saturday 2 October 1937, won by R. Stride, Jnr., with E. S. Stimpson fastest. This was held at Wimbledon on Saturday, October 2nd, in fine weather and a good size field turned out. Actually there would have been an even larger field, but quite a good number went out for a training spin, including among them most of the club cracks. Although it is as yet early in the season for racing; in the old days it was always considered good fun to take part in this race, whatever the result, but with the march of progress, perhaps, different tactics are now required. As to the race itself: George Tyrer went off with his usual long start, with George Still going off next, and George managed to keep in front until nearing home. He was then passed by R. Stride, Jnr., a very promising young runner with a fine stride (excuse the pun!) and he made good use of his start to run home an easy winner. Freddy White showed that marathons had not taken all his pace and ran well to gain second place; with a newcomer in R. W. Johnson just beating Bert Smith for third honours. Ted Stimpson put up the fastest actual time. He was the last to start and worked his way through the field in fine style. Another to show good form was J. A. W. Kemp, while K. N. Wood made a welcome re-appearance to do third fastest time. These three were the only ones to get inside 15 minutes, and when one considers the times of the good old days it will be seen what tremendous improvement our runners have made. e: Belgrave Harriers v. Tyrian Club v. Southgate Harriers
items.s: Race v. Tyrian Club at Coulsdon. Report of a 5-mile race at Coulsdon on 23 October 1937 against the Tyrian Club and Southgate Harriers, won by Belgrave 43 pts., with the placings of the Belgrave runners. On October 23rd we visited the S.L.H. quarters for a race with the Tyrian Club, which consists of past and present members of the London University. Southgate Harriers were also present to contest a match over 5 miles. Although raining all Friday night and best part of Saturday morning, we arrived at Coulsdon in sunshine; but our joy was short-lived, as on our way to the starting point the rain came down in sheets, and with a driving wind both officials and competitors were soon soaked to the skin. Jimmy Kemp, evidently feeling robust, was soon up in the front, together with Les Cohen, and they kept in the lead most of the way. Nearing home Penny and Footer came along and with Cohen going slightly off the trail, these two and Kemp eventually came home together. Scoring 7 aside, varsity system, the points resulted: Belgrave H. 43, Tyrian Club 88, Southgate H. 100. We have to thank our hosts for a very jolly Tea which we all enjoyed after the run. items.sum: Cross-country column by the Running Hon. Sec. previewing the 1937-38 winter fixtures, including the first home race against L'Union Sportive Metropolitaine and the hope of regaining the English title.
e: South of Thames District Team race
Surrey County Youths Cross Country Championship
items.s: Over Plough and Country. Cross-country column by the Running Hon. Sec. previewing the 1937-38 winter fixtures, including the first home race against L'Union Sportive Metropolitaine and the hope of regaining the English title. The Cross-county Season is now well into its stride and the attendances at Belgrave Hall, Wimbledon, are well up to previous seasons. The mid-week runs at the "Rising Sun" are also being well supported and I hope all our members will appreciate how helpful these mid-week runs can be. We use a course which is ideally suited to cross-country training, and, moreover you have the opportunity of training with several Internationals, who are always pleased to give you the benefit of their long experience. On November 13th, at Dartford, will be held the South of Thames District Team race. Owing to the various barring clauses, we have to call on more or less our junior runners, but this season we seem to have a team that should improve upon our second place of last season, With our own Harry Parker as President of this Association, I am sure none would be more pleased than he at a Belgravian success. The following week, November 20th, we have the usual Inter-Club run with Mitcham A.C., Croydon H. and Epsom H. This year we are only holding the one meeting which will, in turn, go to each club's quarters. Actually Mitcham were going to act as hosts for this race, but owing to their restricted dressing accommodation they have asked us to hold the run from Belgrave Hall. I wonder how many clubs have such quarters as ourselves? Lucky is he who joins the Belgrave, and with the gradual advance of the builders upon open country it will soon become a question of suitable country to run on. Here, again, we are extremely fortunate in having the fine open Wimbledon Common, with the lovely stretches of Richmond Park for our members to run over. On November 27th we hold our annual Open Walk from Belgrave Hall and, owing to the large entry, we always arrange an away fixture for our runners. It is taboo for any runners to go to Wimbledon, at least for a run. If they wish to give a hand with the walk, I am sure our Walking Hon. Sec., Alf. Harley, will be pleased to have their names. We have, accordingly, fixed an away fixture with Highgate Harriers, who are also entertaining the R.A.F. Uxbridge, and this will take place from their quarters at De Bohun Farm, Southgate. It is some time since we last visited Highgate, but we are always pleased to meet a club with such a fine record over the country. On December 4th we are holding the Surrey County Youth's Cross Country race over a 3 miles course at Wimbledon. The last time we held the race from our quarters we also provided the winning team; so I trust our junior members (this race is open to those under 18) will turn out and duplicate this performance. If those who are qualified will kindly send me their names, I can send them full particulars. Then comes what is going to be a red-letter day in the Club's history. On December 11th we entertain a foreign club to a race over the country—our walkers are also meeting their walkers—and I think this is the first time that such a fixture has ever been arranged in this country. Our opponents are none other than the very good hosts of our Paris trip last season, L'Union Sportive Metropolitaine. We hope to give them as good a time as our lads had over there, and also give them a run over typical English country. On this day we hold our 7 miles race for the "Blackstaffe" Shield and the race with our visitors will be held in conjunction. There will be the usual Sealed Handicap open to our own club members, so be sure to enter and have a run against some foreign opposition. On December 18th, we are holding the Club Junior Cross-country Championip for the "Savage" Shield. This is over our 5 miles course and is open to all under 21 years of age. On the same afternoon we entertain Ealing Harriers and the Metropolitan Police A.C. to a run, and this will give a chance for some of our newer members to show their paces. The following Saturday is Christmas Day, and we take this early opportunity of wishing all our members a Very Happy Christmas! On Boxing Day morning we hold the usual meeting at Battersea Park track at 11 a.m. The events are all handicap races—120 yds., 2 miles Run, 3 miles Walk. To those sprinters who have been doing some winter training at Wimbledon, this should prove a good opportunity of proving whether it has helped them or not. The cross-country men always turn out in large number for the two miles run; and the "snaky" ones, who have dined wisely over the holiday, usually reap their reward. Entries should be sent to me at least a week before for handicapping purposes. Entry fee for each race is 1/-. The first Saturday in the New Year is also the first day of January, and we welcome to Wimbledon the Dartford Harriers, a very well-known Kent club. Also the Guards Depot, Caterham, are coming along and we hope they will enjoy our country, also the amenities of Belgrave Hall. January 8th is County Championship day, and the Surrey race is being held at Coulsdon from the S.L.H. quarters. I notice that Penny and Footer are already being tipped as probable winners and with such a fine send-off we should have no difficulty in securing team honours once again. We have won this Championship for the past five consecutive years, and eight times out of the last nine years. Also on this day is the Middlesex race, in which we have several members competing as members of the Cadogan A.C., and we wish them every success. A week later, the 15th, is held the Surrey Junior C.C. race; this time at Shirley, which is just outside Croydon. The age limit for this race is 21, and as holders of this title, we hope that this year's team will do their best to retain the honours. The Inter-Counties Cross Country race is due to take place on January 22nd, at Gatton Park, Merstham. We usually provide the bulk of the Surrey team, while our members are also seen in the vests of Middlesex and Kent, so that on the whole there is quite a good Belgrave flavour about this race. On January 29th we hold our 10 miles C.C. Championship for the "Macher" Shield. Last year, Jim Ginty provided a surprise by winning, but whether Jim will defend his title is doubtful, owing to the fact that now he is out of the Army, his job has taken him some distance away from us. We all hope he will be able to turn out for us once again; and lead our team as he did in last year's National race; and we can be sure that he will make every effort to do so. For those who are on the fringe of our senior team I would remind them of the sealed handicap which is held in conjunction with this race. At this time of the season out teams will more or less have taken shape, and we hope that this time there will be no breakdowns or other unforseen contingencies which will prevent us from regaining the title of English Cross-country Champions. That we have the men to do this no one will deny, and although beaten by a mere 4 points last year (and that with our sixth man scoring 41), I feel sure that given reasonable good luck and an even share of the breaks of fortune which in the past has not smiled too freely on us, we will bring the title back to the South once again. items.label: February 1938
items.sum: Editorial notes congratulating Harry Churcher on five Open Seven Miles Walk wins and the walking teams, previewing the championship season, the W. A. Rice Memorial Trophy fund, the French visitors at Wimbledon and club kit.
items.s: Editorial notes congratulating Harry Churcher on five Open Seven Miles Walk wins and the walking teams, previewing the championship season, the W. A. Rice Memorial Trophy fund, the French visitors at Wimbledon and club kit. Our very heartiest congratulations have been earned by Harry Churcher on his sequence of five wins in Open Seven Miles Walks this season. The manner of the accomplishment and the ease with which Harry has won have been features of the season, and called forth praise from all directions. This succession of triumphs is probably a record in the annals of Walking, and we hope to see our man win the A.A.A. 7 Miles Championship, and next season repeat his very fine winning sequence in open road events. * * * * * Our teams also have been very successful and five scratch team wins have been recorded in the five 7 Miles Open events. These wins have been very emphatic and have always been well backed by others who could still have made sure of a team win, even if those in front had faltered. A glance at the Walking results included in this issue will show how complete has been our monopoly of the early placings in the open events, and also indicate the considerable improvement made by some of the younger walkers and newcomers. We trust the forthcoming championships will prove equally successful for our teams! * * * * * The Championship season for both runners and walkers is about to start, and we confidently expect all our supporters to assist by turning up at the various events. Incidentally, a helpful comment is appreciated much more by a competitor than all the alleged humour you have to offer. An idea of position, number of club team men in front, etc., may do something towards winning the race. In our last issue we announced that a fund had been formed to provide a "W. A. Rice" Memorial Trophy. Some of Bill's friends promptly expressed their desire to be associated with this; and others, no doubt, will wish to do so before the fund is closed. No subscription list will be circulated, but those wishing to identify themselves with the plan are invited to get into touch with A. A. Harley within the next few weeks. Subscriptions have ranged between 1/- and £2 - 2 - 0, and we have no doubt that many who came under the influence of Bill's personality, appreciated his work for the Club, and enjoyed his friendship, will associate themselves with the idea before the fund is finally closed. * * * * * We were very glad to welcome our French visitors to Wimbledon on December 5th; also the Mayor and Mayoress of Wimbledon, who accorded the visitors a civic welcome. Our thanks are also due to Frank Elson, who presented the Club with copies of an excellent souvenir programme, which realised something towards the expenses. We should also be lacking in gratitude if we did not thank our Social Hon. Secretary for the special attention he gave to the planning of a very fine meal and Social after the race; and L. J. Coleman for his invaluable services as Interpreter throughout the visit of our French friends. * * * * * See you at the "Southern" at Ascot?—the "Junior" at Hampstead Garden Suburb?—the "National" at Reading? And also don't forget the Senior R.W.A. 20 miles Championship at Birmingham on May 14th! * * * * * Club ties, vests, badges, etc., may be had from the Hon. Treasurer, whose address appears on page 1. items.label: February 1938
items.sum: Notice that the Annual Dinner-Dance at Gatti's Restaurant on May 7th will go ahead although the News of the World has moved the London–Brighton Relay to the same date.
items.s: The Annual Dinner-Dance. Notice that the Annual Dinner-Dance at Gatti's Restaurant on May 7th will go ahead although the News of the World has moved the London–Brighton Relay to the same date. Our Annual Dinner-Dance will take place at Gatti's Restaurant, William IV Street, Strand, on Saturday, May 7th. Most unfortunately, the "News of the World" have, at the last minute almost, changed the date of the London—Brighton Relay from that originally fixed to May 7th—the date of our Dinner-Dance. In reply to our letter of protest at this late change of date, the organisers have replied regretting the inconvenience caused and saying that it is now impossible to alter their revised date. The letter concludes by saying that it would add greatly to our function if we could win the Cup earlier in the day and have it on the table in the evening! An attempt has been made to fix an alternative date for our Dinner-Dance but, of course, to arrange another Saturday date at this late stage has been found impossible. Accordingly, we intend to carry through our arrangements for May 7th, and have no doubt that every Club member will loyally support the Club Function. It is hoped to make some arrangements to enable members of our team to be back in London in time for the Dinner and Dance. It is most unfortunate that we should have been placed in this dilemma so late in the season, and we look to every Club member to make our Annual Dinner-Dance the success it deserves to be. London to Brighton Relay Gatti's Restaurant Strand London

On October 30th, we found ourselves once again at Sheen Schools, undressing to a background of Nursery Rhymes and Fairy Tales. I might say that even at this early stage our boys were in a class by themselves! A big field lined up for the start of the match and after two laps of the starting field the course lay through a narrow path to the gates of Richmond Park. The leaders kept the pace very snappy and the field was soon well extended. Our prospective S. of T. "Junior" men were prominent throughout. The actual leaders, Mason, of Thames Valley H., and Tom Carter had a duel for individual honours, with Mason showing himself the faster man at the finish. items.s: Race versus Cambridge University H. & H., S.L.H., and Aldershot Command A.C. Report and results of the November 6th race at Wimbledon against Cambridge University, South London H. and Aldershot Command, won by Cambridge's E. C. Weir, with Belgrave winning the team race and a club handicap won by Dan Patience; A. Smith's handicap time is printed 22 29 although his times give 33 29. At Wimbledon, on November 6th, we entertained a team from Cambridge University, also members of the South London H., and Aldershot Command H. The spectators witnessed a very fine race and over our rather light course the two Cambridge "Blues," E. C. Weir and W. M. F. Hudson, ran right away from our lads to finish an easy first and second. Arthur Penny ran well to gain third place, with Bert Footer and Dan Patience next, followed by Les Cohen and Tom Carter. Thus it will be seen our boys packed extremely well in the team race and we won fairly comfortably from Cambridge, with S.L.H. beating the Army lads for third place. It was the first time that any of these clubs had visited our quarters at Wimbledon and we trust they enjoyed their run with us, and look forward to renewing associations next season. In conjunction with the race we held a club handicap and this was won by Dan Patience. Much to everyone's surprise the Handicapper gave him 2 mins. start and Dan certainly made the best use of it. There was a tie for second place, this being between H. G. Verney (1.45) and Rod Patience (2.45). Both of these ran extremely well in the scratch race and well deserved their handicap awards. It was a pleasure also to see Sgt. Cotterell, the ex-Southern champion and English International, turning out for the Aldershot boys and they should gain much useful advice from such an experienced performer. RESULTS. Pos. Name. Act. e: South of the Thames Junior Cross Country Championship
items.s: The South of the Thames "Junior Race." F. R. Webb's report of the South of the Thames Junior cross-country race on 13th November, won by Eastleigh Town S.C., with Belgrave's "A" team fifth. BY F. R. WEBB. Saturday, 13th November. Whether it was the date, or lack of voices with that familiar cry of "Up the Bels" was responsible for our team's failure to get placed in the above race I cannot say; but the support they did have must have been the poorest ever. However, the few that did go witnessed a most exciting race. The course, which was one of three laps consisting mainly of grassland. Harry Parker, one of the Club's officials, being President of the South of the Thames Association, had the honour of starting the race. It was also hoped that he would present the Shield to our Club as the winning team, but it did not materialise. Our boys got away fairly well and the field, having covered about half a mile of level going, came to a stretch of plough. After getting over this, they then continued out into the country, and thence back to the starting field, which was preceded by a slight rise, which upset those who had made too fast a start. The first to appear was a bunch of about six runners. A little further back came Tobin in 12th position, followed by Lucas 19th, Morrell 22nd, and Murdoch 36th. Our next man was round about the 50 mark. On their next appearance they had covered about 3 miles, and Roberts, of Mitcham, was leading by a few yards from Isted, of Westerham ,and Shirley, of Ashcombe. Our boys had failed to improve their positions. In fact, they had lost some! Tobin was still our first man, and had lost a few places, as had Lucas and Morrell. Murdoch had gained, so had Clements and Stride. These two were running very strongly and we still hoped there might be a chance of a place. Herbert and Selby were definitely below their usual form, running in 102nd and 113th positions. Johnson, who was in the "B" team, was going very strongly in the 80th position. Again the runners entered the starting field and commenced the last lap; but no claret and gold vests could be seen in the first twenty places. So came the end, with Clements running strongly over the last lap to finsh 18th. Tobin (24th), Murdock (25th) and Lucas (26th) completed our team, which was placed 5th. Eastleigh Town S.C., who owe much to our old friend Tommy Green, were the winners. As previously mentioned, our "A" team finished fifth with 93 points. Our "B" team scored 410 points, and "C" team 663. There were 270 starters, 254 of whom finished the course. F. R. Webb F. R. items.label: February 1938
items.sum: Report of the inter-club race with Mitcham A.C. from Belgrave Hall, won by Belgrave 364 pts. to 456 with Arthur Penny first home.
items.s: Inter-Club Race with Mitcham A.C. Report of the inter-club race with Mitcham A.C. from Belgrave Hall, won by Belgrave 364 pts. to 456 with Arthur Penny first home. This fixture took the place of the usual four-cornered social run with Croydon H., Epsom H. and Mitcham A.C. It has been decided to hold one fixture each season, this to take place in turn from each club's quarters. Owing to Mitcham's quarters being on the small side, we held this year's race from "Belgrave Hall"; and a good crowd was seen out, although Epsom and Croydon were unable to field sufficiently large numbers to count in the team race. So we had a race with the Mitcham boys and, scoring 20 aside, came out on top by 364 pts. to 456 pts. First man home was Arthur Penny; followed by S. O. A. Palmer and R. Thorogood, both of Mitcham. Then came Tom Carter, Les Cohen and Harry Verney, of the "Bels"; followed by L. Scott, of Mitcham, with that old war-horse Bert Footer next. After that, positions were more or less equally divided between the two clubs, although our boys seemed to pack in small groups and this undoubtedly helped when the final scores were worked out. Whether we can take this as a good omen as regards the later "big" races remains to be seen, as in fairness to Mitcham we must say that they did not have their full complement of Welshmen running for them in this race, and there is no doubt that the influx of their "Hospital" boys makes them a much more formidable proposition. items.sum: Report of the November 27th match at De Bohun's Farm, Southgate, won by Cpl. Hier of the R.A.F., in which Belgrave dead-heated with Highgate Harriers in the team race.
items.s: Race v. Highgate H. and R.A.F., Uxbridge. Report of the November 27th match at De Bohun's Farm, Southgate, won by Cpl. Hier of the R.A.F., in which Belgrave dead-heated with Highgate Harriers in the team race. On November 27th we visited De Bohun's Farm, Southgate, for a match with Highgate Harriers; and fellow visitors were the R.A.F., Uxbridge, and the Metropolitan Police A.C. In a race over six miles, Cpl. Hier, of the R.A.F., came home an easy winner, and will prove an asset to Surrey A.C. when the open races come along. Tom Carter finished second with E. W. Bourne, of Highgate, third; and in the team race we dead-heated with the home club, each side scoring 112 pts. The R.A.F. scored 212, and the Police 354. Dick Tobin ran well to be our second man home, followed by G. Murdock and Tom Morrell. Nine aside scored in the team race, and we were very pleased to renew old associations by this pleasant fixture. items.label: February 1938
items.sum: Report and results of the Club 7 Miles cross-country championship for the Blackstaffe Shield on December 11th, run over 6 miles against visitors L'Union Sportive Metropolitaine of Paris, won by A. W. Penny with R. E. Stride, Jnr. winning the sealed handicap.
items.s: The Club 7 Miles C.C. Championship. Report and results of the Club 7 Miles cross-country championship for the Blackstaffe Shield on December 11th, run over 6 miles against visitors L'Union Sportive Metropolitaine of Paris, won by A. W. Penny with R. E. Stride, Jnr. winning the sealed handicap. On December 11th we held the Club 7 Miles Championship for the "Blackstaffe" Shield, with the usual sealed handicap in conjunction. This year, however, marked a very special occasion, none other than the first visit of a foreign club to compete against our boys on their own soil. At the visitors' request the course was one of 6 miles, but the Committee decided that it should still rule as the Club Championship, and so this year's winner of the "Blackstaffe" Shield had less distance to run than usual. Our visitors were the runners of the L'Union Sportive Metropolitaine, Paris. They sent 7 men and so it was decided to score 6 men aside in the team race. The course was the usual one of 2 laps, but, as explained, it was shortened slightly by cutting off a piece out in the country, so that from a spectator's point of view the runners were seen at the usual points of vantage. On the first lap the Frenchmen broke away in a body to go in front, but Pat Parker soon strode ahead only to give way to Arthur Penny and when they came round the first time, Arthur was well in front and running strongly. Dan Patience had come up to Pat Parker, and then came Les Cohen and Bert Footer followed by Tom Carter and then the Frenchmen, running more or less in a solid bunch. When they came in sight again at the Windmill, Arthur Penny was still leading, with Dan Patience a comfortable second, and Pat Parker third. Les Cohen and Bert Footer were still close together, but four of the "Metro" boys had come up to Carter's shoulder, and the leader of them appeared quite fresh. In the run home the positions remained unchanged but Tom Carter fought well, and although having to give way to two of his rivals he managed to fight off the others and finished just in front of three more "Metro" lads. Thus although the Frenchmen packed very well it was too far back to give any chance of success in the team race. With the first five men home our position was unassailable, and our captain, Tom Carter, completed our scoring team of six men which we had in the first eight positions. We are sure, however, that our very good friends from Paris learnt a wrinkle or two which should stand them in good stead in future races. The winner of the sealed handicap was a very promising young runner, R. E. Stride, Jnr., and on his running in the scratch race, he well deserved his victory. J. C. Smart, who is a first-claim member of the Orion Harriers, finished second on handicap; while third place was gained by Dick Michael, who is better known as a track runner. With a Tea and Social Evening after the run we thus ended what was quite an event in the history of our Club, and hope that in future years we may hold events of a similar nature, which do much to cement the good feeling and fellowship between athletes of different countries. items.s: The Surrey County C.C. Championship. Report and result of the Surrey County cross-country championship, won by Mitcham A.C. with Belgrave second, followed by a note on Belgrave runners in the Inter-counties Championship at Gatton Park. The most important feature of this year's Championship was that, after many years in our possession, the title passed into another club's keeping—and Mitcham A.C. are the present holders. This was Mitcham's first win and the manner of their winning calls for the heartiest congratulations. They supplied the individual champion, the third man home, and completed their team in 19 scoring positions—excellent running. We were sixteen points behind, and then came a huge gap and Thames Hare and Hounds in third position with over double our number of points. Our team was not disgraced, and our performance of placing twelve men in the first 53 scoring positions was very satisfying. RESULT. * * * * * A fortnight later A. W. Penny and H. E. Footer figured in the winning Surrey team in the Inter-counties Championship held at Gatton Park, and D. Patience scored in the Middlesex team, placed third. C. T. Carter also represented Surrey, and R. W. Tobin figured in the Middlesex nine. items.label: February 1938
items.sum: T. J. Flower's report and result of the Middlesex cross-country championship at Folly Farm, New Barnet, where Cadogan A.C. (Belgrave) regained the Daily Telegraph Cup with 84 points and F. L. Mason of T.V.H. won; the report's placings (17th, 22nd) differ from the printed result (18th, 23rd).
items.s: Middlesex Cross Country Championship. T. J. Flower's report and result of the Middlesex cross-country championship at Folly Farm, New Barnet, where Cadogan A.C. (Belgrave) regained the Daily Telegraph Cup with 84 points and F. L. Mason of T.V.H. won; the report's placings (17th, 22nd) differ from the printed result (18th, 23rd). It was a long trek to "Folly Farm," New Barnet, but well worth the trip, as our "boys" regained the "Daily Telegraph" Cup, after a very keen and exciting race . We were all feeling fairly confident before the race, and although Alf Taylor had to drop out early in the race through leg trouble, it seemed to add zest to the others. The spectators saw quite a lot of the race, and with very little effort on our part we were able to see the run at five different stages. The race started in a mad dash and after first 700 yards had been covered, Cpl. Hier and J. Bain led the field. They went out of sight into the woods at this point and we waited patiently for their return. Cpl. Hier still led with Bain, and Mason about 15 yards behind. 50 yards further away came D. Patience (4th) and he appeared to be running very strongly. Then they came thick and fast, but to my surprise Tobin was our second man in the 7th position. Verney was 11th, R. Patience 12th, Smart 23rd, J. Flower 28th, Shields 33rd—very satisfactory for the half-way stage. 85 points for 6—with another close up—was very cheering indeed, and they kept these position round the field and so out again into the woods. On entering, the field for the last 700 yards of the race, F. L. Mason, of T.V.H, held a lead of about 12 yards and running in beautiful style and very fast, gradually drew away from J. Bain, last year's champion, who ran a very gallant race, game to the very end. Unfortunately for him he met a man at the top of his form, who finished not only very strongly but comparatively fresh—a worthy "Champion of Middlesex." After this excitement, I concentrated on the Team Race. D. Patience, after a ding-dong battle over the last 700 yards, forced his way to a 10 yards lead over C. W. Griffiths (an ex-champion of Middlesex) and so finished in the 4th position. Very gratifying to myself, waiting to collect the discs! Then came a T.V.H. man (7th), closely followed by Verney (8th) and Tobin (9th). Then two more "Valley" men, 12th and 16th, D. Patience for the "Cads" very close up, 17th, then J. E. Flower 22nd, followed by yet another "Valley" man, 23rd; and what a relief, Shields and Smart, 25th and 26th respectively. A rapid addition of points gave us 84. The T.V.H. scorer, standing beside me, said, "Our boys scored 96, how did you do, Cadogan?" Feeling as proud as if I had actually scored in the team, I replied, "84 and I think we've won it!" "Well done! and congratulations to your lads," was his reply—very typical of the sporting crowd they are! There was sympathy for Smart, who after running a very plucky race, just missed the winning team by one second. To him I say, "Better luck next time! it's your turn next!" A. Patience surprised the natives by his storming finish. He was told (wrongly) that he was 6th man and he put in a tremendous effort, gaining 15 or more places over the last 700 yards. A. Smith put up his best performance in this race. And so for home, feeling quite content in spite of the rain and a 20 minutes' walk to the station. RESULT. A. E. Taylor did not finish. m. s. 1 F. L. items.label: February 1938
items.h: The International Cross-Country Race at la Croix de Berny, Paris, on 16th January, 1938.
items.sum: Account of Belgrave's trip to Paris for the international cross-country race at la Croix de Berny on 16th January 1938, where the team, the only British entry, finished third behind U.S. Belfortaine and C.O. Billancourt.
e: International Cross-Country Race, la Croix de Berny
items.s: The International Cross-Country Race at la Croix de Berny, Paris, on 16th January, 1938. Account of Belgrave's trip to Paris for the international cross-country race at la Croix de Berny on 16th January 1938, where the team, the only British entry, finished third behind U.S. Belfortaine and C.O. Billancourt. A further invitation having been given by the Union Sportive Metropolitaine for us to compete in the above event was accepted and the following team was chosen to represent the Club: Carter, Cohen, Footer, Patience D., Parker, Penny, Tobin and Verney, accompanied by W. G. Webb and H. Parker as Club Officials. Unfortunately, a very rough crossing awaited the party that left London on Friday, 15th January, and on their arrival in Paris on the Saturday morning all were glad to take a few hours' rest. After an early lunch the party made a rather extensive tour of Paris in a coach kindly provided by the French Club; and later adjourned to their Hotel for tea, and to discuss Bert Footer's programme for their evening's entertainment. It was quite evident that Mr. Footer knew his Paris well and did not require the services of an interpreter who had been placed at the party's disposal. The President and Mrs. Bayliss, accompanied by Mr. Togna, joined the company early in the evening and soon we were to hear the voices of our President, Tom Carter, Bert Footer and Arthur Penny coming over the air from the Radio City Broadcasting Station in Paris, telling the French folk why the Belgrave Harriers were in their gay city. Soon after breakfast on Sunday we were speeding on our way to the Headquarters of the Union Sportive Metropolitaine at le Croix de Berny. This famous organisatiaon caters for sport of all kinds and its hundreds of acres of land all set our for sport are indeed wonderful. I doubt if there is anything like it to be seen in this country. The Club House is a huge building and soon we were taking lunch with hundreds of other competitors. 38 teams were to compete in the Internationl Cross Country Race which included the Belgian Champions (Union St-Gilloise) and Belgrave Harriers as the only British entry. After the parade of the runners the "Off" was given and soon we had the pleasure of seeing Parker leading the field, with the rest of the team, excepting Verney, lying quite handy. Verney, it must be explained, had developed a temperature, and though he persisted in turning out, it was very evident that he was unwell. At 3 miles Parker was still leading, with Penny and Footer coming through to the front. At this stage it seemed, however, that our boys were further back than they should be and one began to wonder if that awful sea-crossing was affecting their running. At 5 miles Parker had dropped to 5th place, and though Penny and Footer were running strongly, and Carter and Cohen striving hard, it could easily be seen that we could not win. The team of Algerians (U.S. Belfortaine) was running wonderfully well, and had 3 men in the first four. Our boys ran very pluckily, however, and were beaten by the narrow margin of 5 points for second place. In the last lap of the race, Penny came up to pass Parker and finished first man for us in the 7th position. Parker finished 9th, Footer 11th, Carter 23rd, Cohen 27th, Tobin 32nd, Patience 34th, and Verney continued gamely to finish 117th. The first team placings were as follows:— I understand that during the race our President was introduced to members of the German, Austrian and Italian Governments. Are the Belgrave Harriers to visit one of these countries for International Honours? I wonder! 1. U.S. Belfortaine 68 points. 2. C.O. Billancourt 104 points. 3. Belgrave Harriers 109 points. 4. items.label: February 1938
items.sum: Report of the club's Boxing Day track meeting at Battersea Park, with a 120 yds. sprint handicap, a 3 miles walking handicap, a 2 miles run and a field event match with the Metropolitan Police A.C.
items.s: The Club Boxing Day Meeting. Report of the club's Boxing Day track meeting at Battersea Park, with a 120 yds. sprint handicap, a 3 miles walking handicap, a 2 miles run and a field event match with the Metropolitan Police A.C. At Battersea Park on Boxing Day morning we held our annual track meeting and, being blessed with fine weather, we had a good crowd and, what is more important, good entries. First came the heats in the 120 yds. sprint handicap and the winners were: Heat 1, A. S. Blunden (5 yds.); Heat 2, S. Lyons (7); Heat 3, A. Mewes (6); Heat 4, F. J. Skelley (5). This pointed to a good final, the odds being slightly in favour of Lyons, a new member, and so it turned out. Skelley ran finely but could not make up his two yards deficit and Stan Blunden was close on his shoulder. The winner looks a very promising sprinter and, provided he does not overdo matters too early in the season, he should prove a very useful addition to our sprint team. The 3 Miles walking handicap provided a rather poor field (that is, numerically) and "Ginger" Coleman had no difficulty in winning from Reg. Elson, with a promising young walker in A. E. Elliott, third. Joe Coleman came under the ban of the judges when well placed, while Percy Wright found his Christmas festivities too much for him and retired. We are indebted to Mr. Askew for so kindly presenting a consolation prize in the fourth walker, the only pity being that there were not more members of the walking section there to battle for it. It must, of course, be borne in mind that several walkers were at Croydon, contesting the annual 18¾ miles Boxing Day Walk. As usual, at this meeting, the most eagerly awaited event was the 2 miles run and a large field turned out for this. George Still was on the limit mark, while Arthur Penny was virtual scratch with 10 yards. George kept in front for several laps but the field gradually overhauled him and with a lap to go things looked very interesting. Arthur Penny had come through in great style but still had a good leeway to make up on the leaders. Dick Tobin was in front with A. Harper hanging on his shoulder and A. H. Orton coming up very fast in third place . Down the straight Tobin increased his lead and Orton could not quite catch Harper, while "Champ" Smith had run well to get fourth position. Arthur Penny finished very strongly and Bert Shaw just pipped him for fifth place, which, considering how close he was to the winner, made Arthur doing a very good performance. In conjunction with the racing events we had a Field Event match with the Metropolitan Police A.C., there being three events and scoring for the first six places in each. We triumphed in the Shot Putt by 11 pts. to 10, S. Jones, of the "Bels," having the best putt of 37ft. 5ins. In the Javelin we again came out on top, this time by 12pts. to 9, and C. A. Melchior had the best throw of 143ft. 2ins., with George Powell third. The final event was the Discus and in this the Police had the first three men and so scored 15 pts. to our 6, their best man being W. Grigg, with 123ft. 6ins. Thus in the final points we lost to the Police by 5 points, they scoring 34 to our 29, but I am sure all those who took part were well satisfied with what was the first fixture to take place at this time of the year, and we look forward to holding a similar contest next year. items.label: February 1938
items.sum: Comment by the running secretary on the cross-country season so far, the coming South of Thames, Southern Counties and National championships, road fixtures, and the clash of the News of the World London–Brighton relay's new date with the Club Dinner.
items.s: Winding Up The Country Season. Comment by the running secretary on the cross-country season so far, the coming South of Thames, Southern Counties and National championships, road fixtures, and the clash of the News of the World London–Brighton relay's new date with the Club Dinner. So far this season, results have not been as we hoped they would, but with the real Championship tests now coming along, we hope that our lads will prove their supremacy over the country. Actually our runners, both Juniors and Seniors, have performed very well; and in the three Surrey County races we have recorded a treble of second places which to some clubs would be very pleasing. Also our members with Middlesex qualifications scored a win in their County race, while running for their second-claim club. The next championship in which we compete will be the South of Thames "Senior" race to be held at Cobham. The course there is rather a heavy one, and not likely to suit our boys, while owing to the numerous and, might I say, tedious barring clauses, we are debarred from fielding what can be termed a representative team. We come then to the Southern Counties Championships (both Senior and Junior) which will be held at Ascot. Shades of "Brown Jack"! What is the world coming to? Alas! the modern trend is to make cross-country running easier in every way. They even have artificial obstacles, and quite possibly they will one year stage a race indoors at Wembley! Seriously, though, there is quite a lot to be said for such a venue as Ascot. The dressing accommodation, with the consequent after-the-race facilities, should be A.1, and I am all in favour of anything which is to the benefit of the competing athlete. The spectators should also have a good view of the proceedings, and the "gate" will also benefit the Association, which possibly is the reason for this hankering after race-courses as venues. In the Junior race I am afraid our team will be rather weak, as R. E. Stride and Bill Lucas, who were our first two home in our club Junior championship, are now both over age. It should, however, provide useful experience to the rest of our Juniors, and we wish them the best of luck. As to the Senior race, we must expect hot opposition from Mitcham A.C. and Surrey A.C. At first glance, Mitcham would appear favourites, but Surrey should not be disregarded, and they usually put up a good performance in this race. With our best team in the field we should, however, give them all a rare old battle and we will leave it by saying "may the best team win." On March 12th the E.C.C.U. hold the "National" championship and this year the race will be staged at Coley Park, Reading. We can be assured that the local committee will make arrangements for everybody, and I hope our Club supporters will travel to Reading on the 12th to see what is, without doubt, the finest cross-country race of the Season. Special buses will run from the station to Coley Park, and the course is one which gives the spectators a constant view of the runners. Last year we lost the title by 4 points, the holders, Birchfield Harriers, having a rare fright before they found victory was theirs once again. This year, we hope the tide will turn, and that we shall regain the trophy which we held in 1935. Our teams have, in recent years, always seemed to give of their best in this race; and we hope that Tom Carter, in his first season as Captain, will have the honour of leading them to victory. I am sure all our lads will give him their loyal support. With such names as Penny, Footer, Ginty, Parker, D. Patience, Carter and Cohen to think of, it will be seen that we have every chance of success to bring the title where it has so seldom been in late years, namely the South. On March 19th will be held the "Round Ilford" Road Relay, and we hope to enter teams, as in past years, and so give all our members a chance of representing the club in "open" team competition. The country season is now at on end and we start road training with a view to the London—Brighton Relay race. On April 9th we had decided to hold our usual 5 miles Road Race with sealed handicap in conjunction, but whether this date will be changed in view of the alteration of "Brighton" date, will have to be advised to members later. In any case I hope all our members will support this fixture at Wimbledon, for as mentioned, there is the handicap to go for, and I shall be glad to receive entries in good time before the date fixed for this race. We now come to what is for us a rather unfortunate happening and that is the fact that the "News of the World," after fixing April 30th for their annual "classic," have at this late date suddenly altered the date to May 7th. It is understood that it is owing to clashing with the annual Stock Exchange walk to Brighton, although why this question was not gone into when the date was first fixed is to be wondered at. As our members are aware, May 7th is the date arranged for our Club Dinner and naturally we cannot expect to have half the club at "Gatti's" and half at Brighton. The matter will be discussed by our Committee and what will happen remains to be seen. It would be a thousand pities if we did not compete in this year's race, after being winners for three consecutive years—a feat not previously accomplished in the history of this event. We lost last year by a bare few yards to Mitcham and had looked forward to reversing this result. Our absence from the race might be misconstrued by some, and it is to be hoped that we shall be able to arrange to compete, although very galling, and absolutely lacking in consideration. items.sum: Covering letter from Paris enclosing the proof of an article for the "Metro Sportif" magazine, followed by that article on the Union Sportive Metropolitaine team's visit to the Belgrave Harriers at Wimbledon.
items.s: A Message From Paris. Covering letter from Paris enclosing the proof of an article for the "Metro Sportif" magazine, followed by that article on the Union Sportive Metropolitaine team's visit to the Belgrave Harriers at Wimbledon. My Dear Sir, I send you herewith the "proof" of an article that I am having inserted in the next number of our magazine, the "Metro Sportif." It is an article concerning our meeting with the Belgrave Harriers, and I would thank you very much if you would be kind enough to check me up on the details that I have mentioned. I hope you will excuse me for troubling you and meanwhile I beg you to accept my sincere thanks and my most cordial wishes, etc., etc. WITH OUR FRIENDS AT WIMBLEDON. THE BELGRAVE HARRIERS. One will read further on, under the heading of "Cross Country," an article describing the visit of our team to England on the 10, 11, 12 December, where they were the guests of the Belgrave Harriers, who, you will remember, were our guests last season at La Croix de Berny. It is not the time or place to criticise the result of our match, which left no illusions, but rather to analyse and see what useful purpose has been gained by our visit, and a reception that will certainly go down to posterity in the annals of our Cross Country section. To give you some idea of how formidable were our opponents, I am going to give you some details. First of all, let us remember that the Belgrave Harriers specialise in athletics, walking and, above all, cross country running. Founded in 1887, they, along with the Birchfield Harriers, are reckoned among the top flight of clubs in England. They were cross country champions of England in 1935, winners of the London to Brighton relay race for 1934, 35, 36, winners of the Surrey County Championship from 1925 to 1937, and this year further added to their laurels by capturing our cross-country championship at La Croix de Berny in 1937. Their Patron is Sir Samuel Hoare, former Secretary of State at the Foreign Office, and former First Lord of the Admiralty, now Home Secretary, who combines this presidency with that of the Lawn Tennis Association of Great Britain. Their active President and Hon. Secy. is our excellent friend, Mr. W. L. Bayliss, who has never failed to put at our disposal his kindly services. The Belgrave Harriers have more than five hundred active members. Their training ground is situated at Wimbledon, a south-western suburb of London which has a population of 65,000 inhabitants, and which is world-famous on account of its famous tennis stadium. Wimbledon, situated at only 15 kilometres from the heart of London, is served by the Southern Railway and also an underground line. In close proximity there are the "commons" (Putney, Richmond, etc.), fine sandy stretches, sprinkled with woods, and many gradients, which lends itself perfectly to the art and training of cross-country running, and other sports among them being the noble one of "Equitation." Well, here we are with them at Wimbledon. After a wet and unpromising morning a complete change came about mid-day, and the afternoon proved to be fine and cold. Here, on the premises which the Belgrave Harriers have just acquired and which they intend to demolish in order to build a model club house, is a big hall, comfortably heated. On the floor a badminton court is marked out. At the moment this hall also serves as a cloak room and leading off the hall are several baths, simple in style, but comfortable and above all, warm; whilst a little further on one discovers the pantry, where all sorts of good things were prepared for the dinner that we all enjoyed in common with the Belgrave Harriers, and its many friends. items.s: Belgrave H. v. Metropolitan Police. Report and results of the field events match against the Metropolitan Police (shot putt, javelin, discus), lost 29–34 on aggregate; the report says S. Jones beat Grigg in the Weight and Belgrave won it 11–10, while the printed shot putt table places McLennon 1st, Grigg 2nd and Jones 3rd with Police scoring more points. Field Events. Our match with the Police proved a success, each side having full teams for each event. In the Weight, S. Jones beat D. L. Grigg (International) by a small margin, enabling us to win this event by 1 point, the score being Belgrave 11, Police 10. The other placings were closely contested, the distances being comparable with Summer performances. In fact, Jones's winning distance is best to date. The Javelin was won by C. A. Melchior, who beat Grigg by over 6ft., George Powell being a close 3rd. S. Jones scored as our third team man. H. M. Quackenbos, our Junior Captain, had an excellent throw of 12ft. 9in. and was actually placed 7th. L. Jackson had an off day, after throwing over 120 ft. consistently on practice. We scored 12 pts. to Police 9 pts. We were beaten in the Discus, the Police gaining the first 3 positions although without three of their best men. They have to thank Grigg for this, as he has coached them during the Winter months. S. Jones was again our best performer with 98ft., Melchior and W. H. Sutton completing the team. Although we won two of the three events, we lost the match on the aggregate., points being Belgrave 29, Met. Police, 34. Conclusions drawn from this match show that if serious Winter training is maintained, together with similar matches, there should be an appreciable all-round increase of ability to the benefit of the members and the Club. The Police have asked for another match to be held at Imber Court in February. Thanks are due to Mr. F. G. Thomson, who acted as Field Events judge. RESULTS. Name. Club. Distance Pos. Again our walkers gave splendid support to this promotion, and once gain our successes were many. With our scoring four in the first nine positions, the team race was easily won. In fact, with five men in twelve, six in fifteen, and seven in 19, we should have made a good show against all-comers combined! By reason of their forward walking our "A" team also took the second handicap team awards. There was also much good walking forthcoming from our "B" team, but on this occasion they returned without reward. Len Coleman, included in the "A" team, finished 29th, and with a seven minutes' allowance, was placed third in the individual handicap. His rapid improvement has given much satisfaction. items.s: Our "Open" Walk. Report and partial result of Belgrave's eighteenth annual open walk on 27 November, won by H. G. Churcher with Belgrave taking the scratch team race and second handicap team awards. Printed slips kept: W. H. Snell's handicap time 56 54 (sum gives 56 34), F. Jarvis '57221', Metropolitan W.C. '319m. 49s.', and two teams both listed as Belgrave H. (D). The last Saturday in November, the 27th, was once again the occasion of much activity for walkers. Our Eighteenth Annual promotion attracted 182 entries, and 22 teams were nominated. No less than 33 Belgrave walkers entered, and we started four teams. The afternoon was cold, but fortunately the fog that had threatened during the morning had lifted, and conditions were quite good when our President started the race. Our walkers were soon seen to be prominent, with Harry Churcher and Fred Redman, of the Metropolitan W.C., contesting the lead. Round about three miles, Harry broke away up the hill and proceeded to build up a big lead. The gap between second and third men at half-way was considerable. It was obvious at this point that no other club was near us in the scratch team race. Eventually, our lads finished H. G. Churcher (1st), C. E. Churcher (3rd), P. G. Wright (4th) and J. G. Coleman (6th)—a wonderfully fine team effort, and additionally, there was some splendid further support forthcoming. Actually, ridiculous though it seems, in the best-supported Open race of the season, Don Brown finished 8th and yet did not score in the team! Bert Clayton, our new member resident at Eastleigh, gave another good display of walking in finishing eleventh. He will undoubtedly prove a great asset when he qualifies for our teams. Len Coleman again showed his promise, and succeeded in taking an individual handicap prize. In fact, the whole race may be considered a testimony to the Club's strength. The individual handicap was won by E. H. Johnson (8 min. 40 sec.) of Surrey Walking Club and the Stock Exchange—a rapidly improving walker. Second came R. C. Pantling (4 min.) of the London Vidarians' W.C., and this club succeeded in winning the Team Handicap race. Our "A" team took the second handicap awards. The result, which is appended, gives ample evidence of the Club's success in the race. The Churcher family, in particular, did well, taking three prizes each! Before concluding, we should like to pay a tribute and express our grateful thanks to Messrs. W. Allen, Askew, Belchamber, Elson and Gordon, for their generous contributions to the Prize Fund; to the R.W.A. officials and others who helped with the organisation of the race, and without whose help we could not carry on; and to the competitors themselves for their annual support. items.s: The Club "Junior" Open Walk Championship. Report and result of the club junior walk championship for the Horwood Cup over seven miles on 11 December: Harry Churcher first overall, Colin Sutton junior champion, French walker Cambrai sixth, and "Jock" Ogilvie winning the handicap (H. G. Churcher's printed times 55 30 / 9 10 / 56 20 duplicate E. G. Cornish's). On December 11th we had hoped to welcome a team of French walkers to an inter-club event, to be decided with all club members competing and with the Club Junior Championship for the "Horwood" Cup, in conjunction. Unfortunately, as the day approached, our French friends intimated that they would not be able to send a complete team, but that Cambrai, a well-known walker on the other side of the Channel, would represent them. Cambrai quickly went to the front when the Mayor of Wimbledon started the race, in company with our fastest men. He soon found the pace too fast, however, and eventually finished in sixth position. This does not represent his true form, for he has shown some remarkable pace for an hour, and up to 50 kilometres, in Paris. We understood, however, that he had competed in a long-distance race the previous week, and no doubt this occasioned some loss of speed, if a time of 57 min. 25 secs. over our seven miles course deserves this description. The actual winner, Harry Churcher, won reasonably easily from Percy Wright, who made a good show. Then came the "Juniors," battling out the Championship—probably one of the finest fields seen out in this race. After a most strenuous struggle, Colin Sutton gained a narrow win over Joe Coleman. Bert Clayton, our Eastleigh member, took the third medal in his first appearance in the Club Championship. Form throughout was most satisfactory. Len Coleman would probably have given a better performance had he not devoted the previous evening and the Saturday morning to the care of the French visitors, to whom he acted as interpreter. It was pleasing to see a comparative newcomer in "Jock" Ogilvie take the handicap first, with G. S. Doubleday, another newcomer to walking, in third position. Second prize went to Reg Elson, an old-timer showing a welcome return to form. Act. Pos. Junior Champ. Name. H'cap Pos. 1 H. G. Churcher 55 30 9 10 56 20 2 P. G. Wright 56 26 2 25 54 1 3 1 C. F. items.s: The Ashcombe-St. George's A.C. Open Walk. Report and result of the Ashcombe-St. George's A.C. open walk over seven miles from Sheen Schools into Richmond Park on 2 January, where Belgrave took the first five places; several printed handicap times do not agree with actual time minus allowance (H. G. Churcher, R. F. Elson, E. G. Cornish, W. G. True, W. T. Brunning). Held from Sheen Schools over a seven miles course into Richmond Park on January 2nd, our boys showed their liking for familiar roads by recording a truly amazing performance. Recent form has made us expect some good walking from our teams, but to finish the first five men home in a race of this nature is deserving of a welter of superlatives. Harry Churcher scored his usual win in comfortable fashion, and Len and Joe Coleman finished together, equal second. To say that Joe walked wonderfully well is to invite rhapsodic language to describe brother Len's performance and we will content ourselves with reminding our readers that fifteen months previously Len Coleman won a Club novice race! Captain Charlie Churcher finished in fourth position, and Percy Wright was fifth. Actually there is no scratch team race in this particular event (only a set of prizes for fastest team not gaining handicap awards) or Percy would have found himself in the unique position of finishing fifth in an open race, and yet not scoring in his Club team. Reg. Elson confirmed his recent good form by finishing 10th, and here we would like to record our appreciation of the good nature and splendid sportsmanship of one of our second-claim members, W. E. Ives. Elson was awaiting the return of his shoes from the repairer, who had undertaken to have them at the dressing room in time for the race. Unfortunately, he failed in this, and Reg Elson was ready, all but for shoes. Ives, himself stripped ready to race, hearing of the position, insisted upon the faster man using his shoes, with happy results. We are all grateful to Ives for his self-sacrificing action. In the handicap team race our "B" team was second. This team consisted of Doubleday, Ogilvie, Roberts and True, the two first-named taking their first team prizes in Club teams. Our "A" team was placed third; and so we may be considered to have had an excellent Saturday afternoon out. RESULT. 91 finished. items.label: February 1938
items.sum: Walking notes previewing the Junior and Senior championships, reviewing the Boxing Day Godstone walk, with a note from the track captain and the walking fixture list.
items.s: With The Walkers. Walking notes previewing the Junior and Senior championships, reviewing the Boxing Day Godstone walk, with a note from the track captain and the walking fixture list. At this time of the year, all with any interest in walking turn their thoughts towards the "Junior" Championship, to be held this year from Hampstead Garden Suburb, on March 5th. It is not our usual custom to laud our prospects to the skies; but this year we should be false to ourselves if we did not recognise that we have an outstanding team to represent us. The form of past weeks indicates that we have a team which may well set up a new "low-points" record and better the scores of Surrey Walking Club (1929, 22 points), and our score of 1933 (26 points)—the two best yet recorded. Certainly it is true to say that practically every other club expects us to win the Championship once again, and our boys will do their utmost not to disappoint them! All being well, our first team will consist of A. H. Bridger, J. G. Coleman, L. J. Coleman, R. F. Elson, E. C. Heather, S. C. Roberts, W. H. Snell, C. F. Sutton. All are certain to show a high standard of performance, and we have hopes of supplying the individual champion. We shall also have a second team in the field and we can be sure that they will also make a good show. For the benefit of those who do not fully understand the term "Junior" as applied to this race, it is as well to point out that this has nothing to do with age. A member of a winning team; winners of A.A.A. first-class and R.W.A. first-class standard medals; and members of placed teams in the "Senior" 20 Miles Championship (together with one or two other qualifications), debar a walker from competing in the "Junior" Championship. One can always depend upon a good-class field, despite the various barring clauses; and it is the ambition of every walker to obtain his "Junior" gold medal. We hope that our team will receive plenty of support. The ten-mile course is of three laps, and presents plenty of opportunity to see the race. The journey is easily made by Underground to Golders Green station, thence a 1d. bus fare going towards Finchley, to Willifield Way. The dressing rooms will be at the Metropolitan W.C. Headquarters at the Hampstead Garden Suburb Club. We expect to see many Belgrave members there to give an encouraging word to our walkers; and, we trust, to see and help them record the Club's sixth win in this Championship, which carries with it the "Garnet" Cup. * * * * * And meanwhile, what of the Senior 20 Miles Championship to be held on May 14th at Birmingham? This is still the most important event of the Walking calendar, and we hope to succeed in our efforts to take this Championship once again. In recent years the title has eluded us, although we have always been in the placings and on occasions lost the Championship by one and two points only. In 1938 we should like to make the Championship ours again, and we trust all our walkers will consider how they can help to this end. We have the nucleus of a wonderfully good team and with conscientious training and the determined endeavour to do well, nothing can stop us. Up to the time of writing, our season's walking successes have been many, and it would be a very fitting conclusion to the Winter season if we were able to regain the "Senior" Championship. * * * * * It grows more and more obvious year by year that the Boxing Day Godstone-and-back walk of 18¾ miles is misplaced in the present calendar of walking events. It carries, of course, a large amount of traditional interest and as such always commands a fair entry; but it is very doubtful whether many of the entrants train assiduously and show to the best advantage. In fact, a walker intending to follow the season through, from October's 7 miles races to May's 20 miles championship, would be ill-advised to make a special preparation for the Boxing Day race. In the last race held we entered the largest number of any club (with the possible exception of the promoters) and for the first few miles seemed likely winners of the scratch team race. The disqualification of C. E. Churcher, and gradual loss of places by A. H. Bridger as lack of distance training began to tell, dispelled our chances, despite the splendid "second-half" of Jack Bidgood, who eventually finished third. The winner, D. Christie-Murray (S.W.C.) was well away from the others at the finish and recorded 2 hrs. 38 min. 17 sec. for the distance. Our men finished as follows :— Sutton was with the leaders at the half-disance but lost ground later; and one of the pleasing features was the performance of G. S. Doubleday in his first season. The Walking Hon. Secretary has a number of current R.W.A. Handbooks, and these may be had by club-members at 4d. each. * * * * * We understand that England will be represented in the European Games 50 Kilos Walk, to be held in France on September 4th. Bear this date in mind, distance men! * * * * * FROM OUR TRACK CAPTAIN. With one of our most successful Winter seasons almost behind us, we can look forward with anticipation to the Summer fixtures. A full programme of Club handicaps has been arranged, together with our usual Inter-club Scratch Walks, which will take place on Wednesday, June 8th. A big feature of our road success has been the way members have been getting together for training. This is an idea we hope to carry out during the Summer. Collective training every Tuesday, with various packs, will be arranged. It is hoped that a new record will be set up this season in the matter of entries. Bigger fields mean keener racing and an all-round improvement. All the old faces are expected to be seen once more, and, it is hoped, several new ones. It is the duty of every member to see that even the rawest novice gets the encouragement that is so necessary to the beginner. Be ever ready with helpful suggestions and, if in doubt, direct him to the Captain, or any other Club official. Please remember that there is a Captain of the Section for a definite purpose. He is there to give advice, and one should not be nervous of seeking it. * * * * * Enquiries regarding all the various races, scratch and handicap, are welcomed, and every attempt will be made to give the fullest information. So prepare your programme now, and watch yourself progress! * * * * * FUTURE FIXTURES. March 5th—R.W.A. "Junior" Championship at Hampstead Garden Suburb. March 12th—Walk v. Surrey Walking Club : Croydon—Banstead and back (11½ miles). March 19th—Surrey Co. A.A.A. Walk at Wimbledon. Middlesex Co. A.A.A. Walk at Southgate. March 26th—Inter-Counties Walk. April 23rd—Club 20 miles Walk Championship ("R. W. Ricketts" Shield) with sealed handicap, and Match v. Met. Police W.C. May 14th—R.W.A. items.s: With The Juniors. H. M. Q.'s junior cross-country notes: second in the Surrey County Youths' Race, R. E. Stride winning the Club Junior Championship, second in the Surrey County Junior, and Southern Junior prospects. After an absence of several years we entered, once again, for the Surrey County Youths' Race, held from Belgrave Hall on December 4th. Our boys, many of whom were racing over the country for the first time, were undaunted by the snow and sleet and finished a creditable second. RESULT. On December 18th, the biggest field in recent years turned out for the Club Junior (under 21) Championship. The course was altered slightly to cut out the brook but Stride's time of 29 mins. 15 secs. is, nevertheless, of the same excellent standard set by Stimpson and Clements in previous years. Stride became the holder of the "Savage Shield" with something to spare over W. E. Lucas, but there was some close racing for the minor positions. Beer and Edwards ran very well but Selby was right off form. RESULT. In the Surrey County Junior at Shirley, Mitcham ousted us from our position as holders and hopes that Lucas would bag the individual title were dispelled by the heavy cold which he had. However, our scoring four packed within half-a-minute, enabling us to take second place. Our non-scorers did well in their first attempt at a junior title and should improve considerably with the experience gained. RESULT. Our chances in the Southern Junior are not as bright as they have been in the last two or three years, because Lucas and Stride are both too old. However, Beer, Herbert, Edwards, Selby, Shrubb and Boyden should provide a scoring four capable of being placed. The majority of our other juniors are still under nineteen and with the promise they shew may well provide the club with winning teams in years to come. 1. L. C. Gregory Ranelagh H. 20 15 7. N. C.
